The user is able to define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a card type offers, use `show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. card-type is the card type (string) and name is the profile name (string). profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0...255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, type decimal64. default is true or false and indicates whether that profile is the default value. None of these attributes carry a documented default value.

It follows `router-id-mode` on the bgp-instance. Syntax: `add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>]`, with matching set, delete and `show bgp-instance-<instance-id> [description] [vrf] [local-as] [router-id-mode] [router-id]`; also `show bgp`. router-id-mode is a flag indicating the router-id is the loopback IP; values are use-loopback and manual, default use-loopback. So by default the instance takes the loopback IP as its router ID; set router-id-mode manual and supply router-id to specify it yourself. router-id accepts an IPv6 or IPv4 address, but 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. instance-id is a string 1...255, local-as is a number 1..4294967295, description is a string 0...128. Example: `add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback`.

On bgp-neighbor the timer defaults are: connect-retry-interval 120 seconds (range 1..65535), the interval between attempts to establish a session with the peer; hold-time 90 seconds (range 3..65535), the interval a session is considered active without keepalives or other messages, typically 3x the keepalive-interval; keepalive-interval 30 seconds (range 1..21845), typically 1/3 of the hold-time. negotiated-hold-time is read-only, range 0..65535, default 0. Yes, you can authenticate: `secure-session` sets the authentication method to the peer, values none or TCP-MD5, default none, with `password` holding the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII, string 0..80. Set them on `add bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> peer-as <value> [afi-safis] [enabled] [description] [secure-session] [password] [connect-retry-interval] [hold-time] [keepalive-interval]` or on set. session-state shows Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established or Close, default Idle.

The routes to be advertised to the external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. For routes that are not present in the IGP tables you must configure blackhole static routes: set the `special-next-hop` parameter of the static route command to blackhole (`add ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf> ... special-next-hop blackhole`, likewise ipv6-static-route). Once the route exists in the forwarding table, create the bgp-network object with `add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>`, where instance-id is a string 1...255, remote-address is the BGP peer address in IPv4 or IPv6 format (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported), and network-prefix is a decimal number 1..64 or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network managed objects can be configured. Example: `add bgp-network-10/2620:38:4001:192::65/3000::2/64`.

On comm-channel, `mtu` is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when the mode is L3. It is a uint16 with a platform-dependent range: 1280..1500 octets on 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500; for 1830 GX G40 the per-interface-type defaults are 1518 for DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. Set it with `add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [mtu <value>] ...` or `set comm-channel-<name> [mtu <value>]`. Related L3-only attributes: mru 64..1500 octets default 1500, restart-timer 1..10 seconds default 3, max-failure 2..10 default 5, peer-address default 0.0.0.0. mode is L1, L2 or L3, default L3. By contrast comm-eth mtu is a plain 1280..1500 octets, default 1500.

LLDP is off by default: `lldp-admin-status` on comm-eth defaults to disabled, with values tx-only (transmits LLDP frames but does not store remote system information), rx-only (receives but does not transmit), tx-and-rx, and disabled. It cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, `set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx`. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30 seconds. lldp-mgmt-addr-if picks which interface IP is used as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx, is empty by default, and if unset the system uses the loopback IP, else the DCN/AUX IP, else it does not send the TLV. For speed: auto-negotiation defaults to enabled; rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum) defaults to maximum and duplex-mode defaults to full, but both are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled.

Use the global dhcp-relay commands, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode: `set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>]` and `show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]`. `mode` is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation, with values disabled, ipv4 and ipv6, default disabled. `server-address` holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples: `set dhcp-relay mode ipv4`, or in one command `set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3`, and `show dhcp-relay` to view the settings. Per-interface enabling is separate: `set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true`, which obeys these global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns object has `assignment-method`, which indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values; the assignment method can be both manual and dhcp. Values are manual, dhcp and both, with both as the default. Configure it with `set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>]` and inspect with `show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` is the flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. `search` is the DNS-search-suffix name, a string 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear the value. Examples: `set DNS enabled true` and `show DNS`. Individual servers carry their own origin attribute on the dns-server object.

Add one with `add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>]`, where address is the IPv4/IPv6 address of the DNS server; there are also `delete dns-server-<address>`, `set dns-server-<address> [origin <value>]` and `show dns-server-<address> [origin]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The `origin` attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where the entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address was manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute with the set command. Example: `add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp`.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object: `set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>]` and `show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. `dhcp-relay-enabled` enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface and takes true or false, default false; it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global `set dhcp-relay mode ipv4|ipv6` and server-address must also be in place. Examples: `set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true` and `show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled`. The same if-dhcp-relay attribute is listed on the interface object, again false by default and obeying the global settings.

By default it is statically addressed and protected. On `add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> ...`, `ipv4-address-assignment-method` and `ipv6-address-assignment-method` each take static or dhcp and both default to static. `ipv4-enabled` and `ipv6-enabled` both default to true, connecting the interface to the respective stack so it can send and receive those packets. `protection-mode` is the user given protection mode, values unknown (transient, output only), protected (protected by redundant ports) and unprotected (no port redundancy), and it defaults to protected; the read-only `protection-state` defaults to unknown. Other defaults: admin-state unlock (lock, unlock, maintenance), oper-state disabled, alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (only applicable to the DCN interface), if-dhcp-relay false. if-type is one of ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc. Example: `set interface-DCN protection-mode protected`.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does: a monitoring instance periodically pings certain destinations and the result takes action on configured static-routes. Use `add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]`, with matching set, show and delete. `action` is the action taken when monitoring goes into 'failed' state; values none and withdraw, default withdraw. `static-route` is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6) and next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address; the instance will not be active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is the time between two consecutive pings, 0...60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled defaults to true, alarm-report-control to allowed. The route side shows this as monitoring-state unmonitored/ok/failed.

Use `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, with `show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin]` and `delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. The netmask is the subnet specified as a netmask for that address, and only valid netmasks are allowed. The following IPv4 addresses are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). To see the available interfaces, type ? after `ipv4-address-` and the system displays the object completion options. `origin` is read-only, values static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Examples: `add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'` and `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0`.

On ipv4-static-route the `distance` attribute is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, default 1. For a discard route, set `special-next-hop` to blackhole: this parameter exists because routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, but not by BGP itself, so for routes not present in the IGP tables blackhole static routes must be configured. Its only value is blackhole and the default is blackhole. Syntax: `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]`. `advertised` is true/false, default false; when true the route is advertised in the routing protocol, and for OSPF it is advertised as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR. origin is manual or dhcp, default manual. Example: `add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165`.

Almost, but the qualifier differs: IPv6 uses `prefix-length` instead of netmask. Syntax is `add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>`, with `show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin]` and `delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. `origin` is read-only with values static, dhcp and auto-config, default static. To view the available interfaces, use ? after `ipv6-address-` and the system displays the object completion options. Examples: `add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10` and `add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64`.

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use `add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]`, naming DCN-B in the interface parameter; note the VRF bound to that interface needs to match the vrf given on the static route. Example: `add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B` (the equivalent through DCN is `add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN`). Defaults on the route: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), special-next-hop blackhole, monitoring-state unmonitored. Available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode.

Use `show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component: there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each management address must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor; direction is ingress or egress; address-subtype is the type of management address identifier encoding used in the associated address attribute; address is the string used to identify the management address component associated with the remote system, length 0..64, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the integer interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity, string 0..128.

Both retrieve management address information about a particular chassis component, and both carry the same attributes (if-subtype, if-id, address-oid) with the same meanings. The difference is the key and the side. `show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>` keys on an lldp-port plus a direction (ingress or egress), and covers the addresses received on the local system from the remote system. `show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>` has no direction key and reports the management address information from the local LLDP ports, for example `show management-address-local`. On the local command, if-subtype is spelled out as unknown (interface is not known), if-index (identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object) and system-port-number (identifier based on the system port numbering convention), and address-oid, string 0..128, is currently an empty string. Both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, the networking object carries `use-as-source`, the interface to use as the source address. It is a string of length 0..64 with no default (n/a) and is used in both set and show. Syntax: `set networking [use-as-source <value>]` and `show networking [use-as-source]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example of setting the interface to use as source address: `set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT`. Example of viewing it: `show networking`. That is the only parameter on the networking command.

Use `show networking-services`. This command shows the list of network services and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It takes no parameters at all, so the full invocation is just `show networking-services`. It is distinct from `show networking`, which reports the networking `use-as-source` attribute (the interface to use as the source address).

Because next-hop state hangs off the RIB. In `show next-hop`, each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family. For each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, so the next-hop for a prefix is only meaningful within its RIB. Syntax: `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]`. rib-name is a String (length 1..64, pattern '([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*)'), destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface name (for example DCN), and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Example: `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>`. This removes and restarts the ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the command returns without waiting for the restart to complete. The instance id is a string and is supplied as <instance>. The `-f` flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: `clear ospf 1`. To create, modify or delete the instance itself instead, use the ospf-instance commands (`add/set/show/delete ospf-instance-<instance-id>`).

No. The ospf-area object accepts only one area type: `ospf-area-type` has the single permitted value `normal`, and `normal` is also the default. There is no stub or NSSA option. Commands: `add|set ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>]`, `show ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type]`, `delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>`. instance-id is uint8 (range 0..255) and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0`.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask. It is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only, so it has no effect on a non-ABR. Syntax: `add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>]`, `show ... [advertise]`, `delete ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix>`. prefix is an IPv4 prefix (length <= 32) or IPv6 prefix (length <= 128) in canonical form. `advertise` takes true or false and defaults to true (true advertises the summary, false hides it). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: `add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true`.

Yes. `add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]` accepts `version` values ospfv2 or ospfv3, with ospfv2 as the default; version is settable at add and is shown with `show ospf-instance-<instance-id> [version]`. instance-id is uint8 (range 0..255) and router-id is a dotted-quad. The router id source is `router-id-mode`, values manual or use-loopback, default use-loopback. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback, an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. `description` is a String (length 0..128). Example: `add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3`.

On ospf-interface the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related defaults: retransmission-interval 5 s (2..3600), transmit-delay 1 s (1..450), ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255, where 0 means not eligible for DR/BDR), enable true, ospf-if-routing auto (active, passive, auto). Authentication is available: `ospf-auth-enable` true/false, default false (relevant for ospfv2 or ospfv3); `ospf-auth-algorithm` none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256; `ospf-auth-key` an ASCII string of length 0..256. The algorithm and key are only of relevance for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must exist before adding the interface.

Use `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority]` (Operational Mode). The `state` values are: down (initial state, no Hello packets received from the neighbor), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional communication established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor (DBD) packets containing LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs), full (full adjacency achieved). The `role` values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Note: an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use ospfv3-ipsec-security-association: `add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>]`, plus set/show/delete. The SPI is a unique uint32 in range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and takes AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 or AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. ipsec-protocol indicates ESP or AH but the only value is ESP (default ESP), and ipsec-mode supports only transport (default transport). Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: `add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128`.

Use `ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>`. `-i=<interface>` specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. `-v=<vrf>` specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. `-c=<count>` stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, `-w=<timeout>` sets a timeout in seconds before ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and `-s=<pktsize>` sets the octets sent exclusive of headers, default 56, plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total of 64 octets. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Example: `ping -c=1 -w=10 -s=1024 192.0.2.3`.

`show protocols` lists them all in one place. Syntax: `show protocols [ssh|cli|serial-console|netconf|grpc|snmp|restconf|http-file-server|data-model-openconfig]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Plain `show protocols` returns the nine containers: ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. Adding a keyword shows that protocol's detail, for example ssh with enabled and port 8022 plus host keys and pre/post-login messages, cli enabled true on port 22 with script-dir '/storage/scripts', netconf enabled true port 830, restconf http-port 8080 and https-port 8181 with cookie-timeout 5 minutes and api-root '/restconf', grpc port 50051, snmp port 161 with snmp-engine-id, http-file-server http-port 8980 and https-port 8981 with url-base '/transfer', and serial-console global-switch enabled with global-timeout 60 minutes.

Use `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family. rib-name is a String (length 1..64). The `address-family` attribute takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast, and `vrf` is a leafref to ../../vrf/name showing the VRF the RIB is bound to. Example: `show rib-IPv4` displays the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key.

Use `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]`. The `source-protocol` attribute gives the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP or static, so it distinguishes dynamic protocol routes from static configuration. The command shows the list of system routes from various sources, such as dynamic protocols and static routes. rib-name is a String (length 1..64) and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. `special-next-hop` applies to IPv4/IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring, with values none (default, no special treatment, used for all normal routes), blackhole and unreachable; for blackhole and unreachable routes no next-hop is created under the route. Example: `show route`.

Yes. `show routing` shows routing information. It takes no parameters at all and is available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For more detail, drill into the related commands: `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]` for the RIB per address family, `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]` for the route list including its source protocol, `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]` for next hops, and `show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description]` for the routing instances.

`show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface>` shows supporting interface information, that is which underlying IPv4/IPv6 interface supports a given interface. It has two parameters: `name`, the name of the interface (string), and `interface`, a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, expressed as a path with the value ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. Both are used only with show. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]` probes a maximum of 30 hops by default; `-m=<hopcnt>` is uint8 in range 1..255 and sets the maximum number of hops (max time-to-live). The VRF is MGMT by default: `-v=<vrf>` specifies the VRF and, if not provided, defaults to MGMT. `-i=<interface>` sets the source interface, which by default is selected according to the routing table, and the interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. `-w=<timeout>` is uint16 in range 1..10 seconds, default 2. pktsize is the total probing packet size, uint16 (60 bytes for IPv4), default 60. Example: `traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4`.

Use `show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description]`, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. `name` is the VRF name, a String of length 0..32. `chassis-name` gives the associated chassis name for that VRF. `type` reports the VRF type with values mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF). `description` is a String of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. Running `show vrf` without a key lists the instances; to view one, for example the management VRF, use `show vrf-MGMT`.

A successful swimage activation implies a system restart. Syntax: `activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>]`, Operational Mode. The optional `db-action` selects what happens to the database: auto (default) activates the image processing the database with the system default behavior, empty-db activates with an empty database, upgrade-db activates by upgrading the current database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless `-f` is given, the user must confirm the activation when prompted. `label` names the sw image/manifest file; if not specified the currently installable image is used. Example: `activate swimage db-action=empty-db`.

No. Only a single location led test can be running at a time, and not all cards support the Location LED test functionality. Syntax: `activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>]`, Operational Mode. `entity` is a chassis or a card. `led-mode` is flash (default, amber light blinking at 1 Hz, used for LED location) or solid (steady amber, used for lamp test); in lamp test all chassis LEDs light amber. To turn it off use `terminate location-led [entity=]<value>`, or set `timeout` in the range 0..120 seconds; the default timeout is 0, meaning no timeout and the function runs until terminated. Note: the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so use terminate there. Example: `activate location-led card-1-1`.

Use the `bootstrap` command, which establishes a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisions the initial administrator account on a neighbor NE that has no configured users yet. Syntax: `bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Select the neighbor either by `local-port`, the supporting-port of a MGMT vrf osc-eth interface as shown in `show interface` (e.g. 1-1-dwdm-line1), which the system maps to the OCE netdev (OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id>) and resolves into neighbor-address via get_osc_neighbors.sh, or by `neighbor-address` directly, the IPv6 link-local address of the OSC peer including zone (string length 7..256, pattern 'fe80:.*'). If resolution fails the RPC is rejected. `new-admin-user` is mandatory, length 1..32, obeying local user naming rules. `new-password` may be plain text (standard complexity rules apply) or a $<id>$<salt>$<hash> hash, only id 6 (SHA512), salt 2..16 chars.

Type `cancel-upgrade`. The full syntax is `cancel-upgrade [-h]`, where `-h` just displays help for the command. It cancels any active upgrade in progress. Access mode is Operational mode. Pre-condition: an upgrade must be in progress for this command to execute successfully.

`change-ztp-mode enabled` starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so re-enabling it on an in-service node wipes the configuration. Syntax: `change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>` with ztp-mode values enabled or disabled, Operational mode; `-f` forces the command without confirmation, so without it you are prompted first. `change-ztp-mode disabled` disables ZTP and stops ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. Use `show ztp` to display the current ZTP mode configuration. Example: `change-ztp-mode disabled`.

Use `show current-fw-<name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status]` (also keyed as <card-name>-<port-name>, <card-name>.<slot-name> or <chassis-name>-<slot-name>). It compares `fw-version`, the current firmware version, against `expected-fw-version`, the expected version, both Strings of length 0..32. `fw-status` gives the verdict with values current (current firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) and unavailable (firmware status information is currently unavailable); the default is unavailable. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: `show current-fw` lists all, `show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1` shows one card component.

`download` accepts filetype values crl (a CRL in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (PKCS#12 with password-protected private key, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#12), script (a CLI script), swimage (downloads a manifest file then all files belonging to a SW image), and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place; there is no need to provide a local storage location. The exception is filetype 'file', where `destination` may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name only, a relative path or an absolute path, and you must have write access to it; use `show transfer` to see the default storage directory. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp. Source is a URL (ftp, sftp, scp, http, https, file) or a pre-configured file-server plus path; non-secure ftp/http need secure-mode disabled.

Use `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]`, which retrieves information about downloaded image files. The `signature` attribute is the downloaded software image file signature, a String of length 0..1024. The key is the manifest file (String, length 0..256) plus `name`, the name of the downloaded software image (String, length 0..256). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. `show downloaded-image` lists all downloaded software image files.

`show downloads` shows the list of downloads. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands: `show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature]` for information about downloaded image files including the image signature, `show manifest` for the downloaded manifest file and its information, `show sw-management` for software locations, activity and downloads, and `show transfer-status filetype` to check progress of a download started asynchronously with `download -a`.

Use the `file` command (Operational mode): `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>`. Supported operations are rename (renames a file or directory), view (listing for a file or directory), delete (deletes a file), sha256sum and md5sum (hash checksums). new-file-path is only used when operation is rename. Note that file system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files/directories are editable. The `result` attribute reports the file operation result. Separately, `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` removes one particular system file; filetype may be krp (only 1 krp may exist, so target-file is not needed), script, or swimage (deletes a downloaded swimage which was not yet installed). Examples: `file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log`, `file delete /tmp/a.log`, `clear file swimage <manifest>`.

Both perform basic file and directory operations and both run in Operational mode, but `file` is the fuller command. `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>` supports five operations: rename, view, delete, sha256sum (SHA256 hash of a file) and md5sum (md5 hash of a file), and it has a `result` attribute plus the companion forms `show file <filename>` (displays file contents) and `clear [-f] file [filetype=] [target-file=]` for clearing krp, script or swimage files. `file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value>` supports only three operations: rename, delete and view, with the same string file-path and new-file-path parameters and no checksum, show or clear capability.

Configure servers with `add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>]`, editable with `set` and removable with `delete file-server-<name>` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). The protocol values are file, ftp, sftp, scp, http and https; `file` represents local storage including USB storage and requires initial-path to be provided. ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is set to false. server-address may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain name. server-port is optional; if not provided the default for the selected protocol is used. name is 0..64 characters, user-name 0..64, password 0..128, initial-path 0..256 and label 0..256 characters.

Use `show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation]` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). `name` is the file type for which the transfer happened. `last-completion-status` is the last transfer status, `last-transfer` is the last transfer start timestamp as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command), `last-duration` is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, and `last-operation` is the last transfer operation with values unknown, upload or download. For richer per-operation detail including progress and byte counts, use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation>` instead.

Yes, but HTTP is off by default. Use `set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>]` and `show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base]` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). `enabled` is the master switch for file server access, true/false, default true. `http-enabled` is true/false with default false; `https-enabled` is true/false with default true. The default `http-port` is 8980 and the default `https-port` is 8981. `url-base` is the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application, a string of 1..100 characters, default /transfer, and is show-only.

Use the manifest commands (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). `show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` gives the manifest itself: manifest-signature is a hex-string up to 1024, downloaded-on is the download timestamp in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and information is a string up to 256. `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]` gives each package, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version is up to 64 characters and description up to 512. `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` lists the firmware included. `show manifest` lists all manifests.

No. The `packaged-fw` commands show the firmware version included in a software-load, and versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type. Use `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` or `show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> of the SW load subcomponent, up to 64 characters. swload-state is active, inactive or installable. equipment-type is the type of equipment (card, etc) that will use this firmware, up to 32 characters, as are fw-name and fw-version. `show packaged-fw` lists all components' firmware versions in the load.

Yes. `prepare-upgrade` has two options: validate, which validates the software label/manifest, and apply, which applies it. Syntax: `prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> [[db-action=]<value>] [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>`, Operational Mode. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. db-action is valid for unattended upgrade only, with values empty-db, upgrade-db (default) and rollback. clear-type (full default, keep-networking, initialize-from-script) is only valid for an unattended operation with db-action set to empty-db. Example: `prepare-upgrade validate <label>` then `prepare-upgrade apply <label>`.

`clear [-f] recover-mode` clears the recover-mode flag. This action clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. As such, it may be traffic impacting. The command has no parameters; the only flag is -f, which forces the command without confirmation. Access mode is Operational Mode. Examples: `clear recover-mode`, or `clear -f recover-mode` to skip the confirmation prompt.

Use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` with attributes [swload-version] [swload-manifest] [swload-prepared] [swload-status] [swload-information] [swload-activation-type] [swload-vendor] [swload-product] [swload-label] [swload-delta-label] [swload-pkg-type], in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. swload-state is active (active load), inactive, or installable. swload-manifest and swload-prepared (true/false) are only of relevance for the installable load, as is swload-activation-type: direct (no reboot type determined), warmstart (warm reboot) or coldstart (cold reboot). swload-status covers status-unknown, validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed and timeout variants. Examples: `show software-load-active`, `show software-load-1-5/active`.

Use `show software-location-<location-id>`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. location-id is the location of the equipment, a string of up to 64 characters, given as <chassis-id>-<slot-id>. For example, `show software-location-1-5` retrieves software location information for the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To drill into a specific load at that slot, combine it under sw-management, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`, or address the load directly with `show software-load-1-5/active`.

Use `show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which these constraints apply, strings of 1..20 characters. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by this subtype in gbps and max-capacity the maximum in gbps, where -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications and unsupported-applications are lists of application types; if either list is empty, then that constraint is not applicable. description is a string of 1..255 characters.

Use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, or `show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name> ...` without a location, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The `state` attribute is the package state: installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (software package install failed) or unknown (software package state unknown); the default is unknown. So a failed install shows state installation-failed. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> up to 64 characters, name is the package name up to 256, version up to 64 and description up to 512. `show sw-component` lists all components; example: `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`.

Use `show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime]`, which lists the OS-level containers, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. cpu-usage is the current CPU usage by the container in percentage, range 0...100%, and in a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores. memory-usage is the current memory usage in percentage, range 0...100%. state is off (default state, not launched yet), up (container is up and running) or exited. equipment is a leafref to the equipment card AID on which the container is running, and uptime is the time since the container started. `show sw-container` shows all; example: `show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi`.

Yes. `sw-control-rule` adds service-specific custom rules that override the default action upon service failure: `add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>`, `set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>]`, `show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action]`, `delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. service-name is the name of the service to be monitored, a string of up to 64 characters. fail-action values are default-action (performs the policy of restarting the service, then rebooting the system if the service is not recovered), ignore (no automatic action taken on service failure), and system-restart (warm restart of the system/card software immediately upon service failure). Example: `add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action`.

Yes: `show sw-management [downloads | software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] | software-load-active | software-load-inactive]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `downloads` shows the download history (the list of downloaded manifests). `software-load-active` shows the active software and `software-load-inactive` the inactive software, each listing the sw-components and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. `software-location-<shelf>-<slot>` scopes the same view to one card, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`.

Use `show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count]`, or `show sw-services` for all services and containers on the node, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `reboot-count` is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16, so a high or climbing value indicates repeated restarts. Cross-check `last-start-time` (the time of the last service start/boot, date-time YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and `uptime` (time since the service turned up, in days:hours:minutes). `state` is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with state-details giving a brief description. Example: `show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr`.

`sw-subcomponent` drills one level deeper. `sw-component` is keyed by <location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> (or <swload-state>/<name>), whereas `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description]` adds the sw-subcomponent-name key so you see the individual pieces inside a package, for example `show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb` versus `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. The attributes are the same: state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown); version is up to 64 characters and description up to 512. sw-component-name and sw-subcomponent-name are strings of 1..256. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Run `swversion`. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists both the NE-level loads and the per-slot loads with version and label, for example software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188, software-load-inactive R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.04.15_14_26-sim-112, software-load-installable, then software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable. For fuller attributes use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or `show sw-management`.

Use `show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `file-status` is the firmware file status with values valid, invalid or missing. `crc` is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present, a string up to 64 characters, and `path` (up to 255) is the path for the firmware image. `applicable-eqpt` is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to and `present-in-eqpt` is the list of resources that contain this version; both lists have max-elements 80. vendor, part-number and version are strings up to 64, and nsa-upgrade-version (up to 255) lists the versions from where the upgrade is non service affecting.

Set it with `set transfer http-proxy <value>` and read it back with `show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]`, in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. http-proxy is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note that this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string of up to 1024 characters in the format '[http://]<host>[:<port>]', where 'http://' is optional, <host> may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and <port> is optional; if <port> is omitted, the default is 1080. Example: `set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080`.

Use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. transfer-progress is the transfer completion percentage, 0-100, default 0; bytes-transferred and total-bytes are uint64 byte counts, total-bytes staying zero until known at transfer start. operation is upload or download. details gives the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle (default), preparation or transfer. last-completion-status may be success, fail, in-progress or unknown (unknown occurs if the system reboots mid-transfer). In synchronous mode a textual progress bar is rendered live in the CLI; for asynchronous transfers (-a) use this command.

Use `show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Status is reported at the NE level, chassis level and card level; `resource` (up to 255 characters) specifies the object, and for ne and chassis the results are aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so query the NE to see upgrade-partially-failed then the individual cards to locate the failure. status values include idle (default), upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, plus validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, failed and complete variants, and no-communication. `step` (up to 128 characters) identifies the current upgrade step, with step-start-time, start-time and end-time (each 'na' if idle since startup) and details.

Use `upload [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ([destination=]<value> | [file-server=]<value> [[path=]<value>]) ...` in Operational mode. For diagnostics set filetype=debug-log, which uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting and includes all other logs; debug-entity is mandatory for debug-log and restricts the logs to a particular card/chassis, and optional-content adds optional content. Other log types are logs, pm-log, fdr-log and otdr-result. Certificates differ: for local-certificate, peer-certificate and trusted-certificate a specific certificate must be given with certificate-name, except for trusted-certificate where omitting the name exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not, and output files are in P7 pem format. -a uploads asynchronously (track with `show transfer-status`); -s skips TLS or ssh known-host verification.

Use `show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status]`, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. ztp-mode is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled with default enabled, and is set via the change-ztp-mode RPC, which is allowed even when the NBI is locked. ztp-state is the current state of the ZTP service, with default ztp-init and values ztp-init, dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. ztp-details is additional information on the current state, up to 256 characters. ztp-completion-status summarizes completion as not-completed (default) or completed.

Use `show capabilities-<name>`, where name is the name of the card (string, no default). This retrieves the information about that card's capabilities. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For capability data organised by type rather than by installed instance, the supported-* commands cover the same ground: `show supported-card-<card-type>`, `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>`, `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>` and `show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>`.

`add card-<name>` requires three parameters: required-type, chassis-name and slot-name. Optional on add are required-subtype, card-mode, subslot-name, power-profile, alias-name, admin-state, alarm-report-control and label. required-type is the card type, a string of length 0..32, from the supported list (BLANK, CHM1R, CHM2T, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, FAN, FAN-CTRL, IOPANEL, PEM, SPN2, SPN2C, UCM4, UTM2, XMM4, RD20TM, ILAx and so on). chassis-name is a string of length 1..255 with default 1; slot-name is a string; subslot-name (for example 1-2.3, slot 2 subslot 3) can only be set at (sub)card creation. Example: add card-1-4 required-type CHM1R chassis-name 1 slot-name 2.

In 1830 GX G40 the chassis ambient temperature must be set to 40C before a Native ZR TOM will come up. If that parameter is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. Set it with `set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature 40` (it can also be given on `add chassis-<name>`). configured-ambient-temperature is a number in Celsius units with no default, and it is used to compute the FRU's power consumption. Check the current value with `show chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature`.

Use `show console-<name> baud-rate actual-baud-rate auto-sensing-state` and `set console-<name> baud-rate <value>`. Permitted values are auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. In auto-sensing mode the system auto-detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, then locks it; the detected rate shows in actual-baud-rate and auto-sensing-state reports sensing (default) or locked, and is only visible if auto-sensing is enabled. Not all cards support auto-sensing: `show supported-card-<card-type> console-port-support` reports no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate or yes-with-fixed-baud-rate.

Use `show controller-card-<name> redundancy-status redundancy-standby-status number-of-switchover-events time-of-last-switchover additional-details`. redundancy-status is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). redundancy-standby-status reports ready-synchronized (standby controller is sync and ready), not-ready-synchronizing (default, synchronizing data with the active controller), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out state) or card-not-present. It is ready to take over when this reads ready-synchronized. number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card; additional-details is a string 0..128 giving synchronization detail.

`show equipment [<option>]` displays installed equipment information; the available options vary according to your installation. Passing an equipment name filters to that one item, for example `show equipment card-1-1`, which lists the child objects of that card (controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-AUX-2, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) followed by its attributes: required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Only if you enable it. `set equipment-policies tom-auto-migration enabled` turns on automatic update of the TOM subtype based on the present equipment; `disabled` turns it off. This update may have direct impact on existing configurations, and it applies to TOM subtype migration only, not TOM type migration (there is no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). Degrees are governed separately by auto-assigned-degrees (enabled/disabled), which enables automatic degree assignment when a card that supports degrees is provisioned; its default is disabled, and enabled if l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. auto-assigned-directions is a separate flag and is enabled by default. View with `show equipment-policies`.

You have to enable them. `set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>` controls whether serdes-templates are globally enabled; values are enabled and disabled, and the default is disabled. On enabling, templates are not automatically applied to what is already there; they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact: existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, independently of whether it was applied via template or manually. View the flag with `show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates`. Re-application of a template can be forced with the apply-template command.

Use `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>`. This displays the packaged FRU information associated to a particular equipment-type. manifest-file is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; equipment-type is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. Neither has a default. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the inventory commands, which show the inventory data for a present FRU: `show inventory-<name> serial-number clei`, and equivalently `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>`, `show inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name>` or `show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`. serial-number is the serial number of the equipment and clei is the Common Language Equipment Identifier, both strings. The same command also returns hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision (default 0), PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class, actual-max-power-draw and fw-status. Examples: `show inventory`, `show inventory-1-3-1`.

Use `show led-<location>/<name> [status]`, or `show leds` for the full list. The object exists even if the FRU is not physically present, in which case the status reads not-available. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID), a string of length 1..32; name is the LED name within the FRU, a string of length 1..16. status values are: not-available (the default), off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycling between all supported colours including off), cycling (all supported colours excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber.

In 1830 GX G40 there are three types of ports: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports are on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs. The trib/line ports can be seen on a CHM6 or a CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is provisioned in the CHM6/CHM7. `show port-<card-name>-<port-name> port-type` reports the type: line (line-side 'coloured' CWDM or DWDM module), tributary (standard 'grey' client interface), tributary-subport (a tributary split into subports), usb, comm, uplink (aggregation ports connecting to an adjunct line function), optical, otdr, ocm, and pluggable (the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM). Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

Use `show resources-<name> internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth paired-slot-total-bandwidth paired-slot-available-bandwidth`. These parameters are applicable only to SPN2/SPN2C cards, and the paired-slot pair only to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots. The internal cell-switch total and available bandwidth default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability; the paired-slot total and available bandwidth default to 500.000 Gbit/s with that capability and to 0 without it. The same command also returns supported-carriers, unassigned-carriers and supported-sub-components. Example: `show resources-254-1`.

Read the status leaf: `show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value status`. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, with values set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown, the default), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). It has taken effect when status reads set. The parameter itself is created with `add serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>`, changed with set, and removed from the configuration with delete. Example output: serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ, value 1, status set.

A serdes-template is created by the user per tom-part-number (string of length 1..16) and applies to all line cards that support serdes; when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. The port scope is narrowed with ports-applicable, whose values are 'all' (all ports considered, the default) or port names, string length 1..16, maximum 20 elements; card-types-applicable can also be given on add. Application depends on the use-serdes-templates flag being set to true. Manual serdes configuration is still possible and is kept even if it deviates from the template. Switching a TOM for one with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists; apply-template forces re-application.

Each entry is a serdes parameter name plus its value, added with `add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>`. Edit it with `set serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> [value <value>]`, remove it with delete, and view it with `show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]`. name is the name of the serdes parameter, a string of length 0..256, and value is a string of length 0..256. Examples: `add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3` and `set serdes-template-entry-TR-FC85S-NIN/TxEQ value 2`. Entries list as serdes-template-entry-FTLC9555SEPM-NF/RxAmplitude with value 2.

Yes. `set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]` sets the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system, and `show serial-console global-switch global-timeout` displays it. global-switch allows access by serial console, values enabled or disabled with default enabled; each console port can override this global behaviour through the console local-switch parameter (use-global-switch, force-enable, force-disable). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes with default 60, and can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. The serial-console object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80.

Use `show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` (or `show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>` for a subslot) with AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; `show slot` lists every slot in the node. installed-type is the currently installed type in the equipment holder, and if empty it means no FRU is present. supported-type lists the types the holder supports, for example CHM6,gx:UCM4. current-equipment names the equipment currently required in the slot, for example 1-1, and shows --- when nothing is provisioned. For the full list of card types allowed in a slot, use `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> possible-card-types`.

Use `show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]`, or `show sub-component` on its own to list them all. card-name is the name of the card supporting the sub-component, a string of length 0..64; sub-component-name is a string; AID is a string of length 1..64; description is a user configurable description of the sub-component, a string of length 0..128. Example output: sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec and description 'DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component', and sub-component-1-6/dco-secproc with AID 1-6-dco-secproc. `show resources-<name> supported-sub-components` gives the names of the sub-components present in a card that can be addressed for operations such as restart.

Use `show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility`. node-type-compatibility is the supported NE node-type for a sled card and is only of relevance for line-cards and carrier-cards. Its values are all (compatibility with any node-type), ILA (In-Line Amplifier, two-directions) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer). A card usable on an ILA node reports ILA or all. The same command also returns sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. `show supported-card` lists all card types.

Use `show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> controller-redundancy-supported number-of-front-slots number-of-rear-slots`. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether the chassis supports controller redundancy. number-of-front-slots and number-of-rear-slots are uint8 counts of equipment holder slots in the front plate and back plate. chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. Example output for a G42: controller-redundancy-supported true, power-control-supported true, depth 600 mm, height 3 RUs, 7 front slots, 12 rear slots, supported-subchassis-type G42. Also available: supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, fan-adjustment-on-altitude, dust-filter-replacement, leds and supported-features.

Use `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> port-type configuration-mode`, for example `show supported-port-CHM1R/2`. port-type states what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, ocm or pluggable. configuration-mode states who configures it: system-configured (the system automatically configures the card in the slot or TOM in the port and the user cannot make changes) or user-configured (the user can provision or de-provision). The command also returns direction, faceplate-label, leds (maximum 10 elements), present (always, or in-node-controller-only), default-tom (default none), parent-port, subport-list, and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true), which says whether TOMs on this port type are auto migrated according to the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag.

Use `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> requires-blank-when-empty possible-card-types`. requires-blank-when-empty states whether the slot needs a BLANK filler card when empty, with values not-applicable, optional and required. On a 1830 GX G40 (G42 chassis) slots 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and PEM-1 through PEM-4 are required, while slot 2, FAN-1 through FAN-7 and FANCTRL-1 are not-applicable. possible-card-types lists the card types allowed in the slot, maximum 15 elements, for example XMM4 for slots 1 and 3 and CHM6,UCM4 for slots 4-7. The command also gives slot-location (front/rear), slot-vertical-position, slot-horizontal-position, configuration-mode, auto-provision-capable, default-card, reset-power (W at 55C), virtual-slot and leds.

Use `show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> supported-phy-modes default-phy-mode supported-subtype`, for example `show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28` or `show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout`. tom-type is the TOM type name such as CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD, and tom-subtype-group is a string of length 0..32 such as '4x100GE-breakout'. supported-phy-mode lists the phy-modes supported in that TOM for that card, from: 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G, 200G. default-phy-mode is the mode used by default, drawn from the same set. supported-subtype gives the subtypes supported in that particular card/port.

Use `show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> supported-power-class supported-max-power-draw`. supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, uint8 in the range 1..8; the port may only partially support that class, so read supported-max-power-draw as well, which is the maximum power in watts (decimal64) the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class. tom-type is the pluggable form factor, the TOM type identity matching the TOM required-type, for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD. What the installed module itself reports is available as actual-power-class (uint8, 1..8) and actual-max-power-draw in the inventory command, populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules.

Yes. When you create a TOM with `add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>`, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created along with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. required-type is mandatory on add and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set are required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; applicable only to TOMs on CHM7 cards). Example: `add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD`. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show tom-type-<tom-type> support-third-party-toms`. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (false, true) that states whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to the supported Nokia TOMs. The same command also returns description (string 0..255), data-rate (uint16, Gbps), and generic-subtype, which is the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. `show tom-type` with no AID lists all supported TOM types. It is a show-only command, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the tom object, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) exists specifically to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It appears under `show unprovisioned-inventory`, which lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. The AID is `unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>`, where chassis-serial-number is the residing chassis serial number (string 0..16) and slot-name is the residing slot name (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, slot-name is empty. Retrievable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ), and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected that unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]`, for example `show usb-1-5-U1`; `show usb` alone lists every USB port in the node. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free storage and total-space the total storage in the associated file-system, both uint16 in MB. available-space, total-space and usb-path are only applicable when type is storage; type is either storage (file storage plus associated file management operations) or power-supply (powers external equipment such as passive shelves). present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the USB connector is inserted. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` from Operational mode. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken (see take-snapshot) before it can be activated. db-instance names the database snapshot to activate and defaults to temp. The paraphrase is a short description of the database to be activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override overrides the sanity check and takes true or false, defaulting to false. Examples: `activate-snapshot sanity-check-override` and, to activate a snapshot named onehour, `activate-snapshot onehour`. Existing snapshots can be listed first with `show database`.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after `enable-advanced-parameters` on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain your symptoms: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter has been deleted, `show advanced-parameter` reports `ERROR: object does not exist`; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but `show advanced-parameter` reports status `failed` for it. Syntax is `add|set advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>`, with `show ... [value] [status]` and `delete`. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set, unknown (default unknown). Example: `add advanced-parameter-1-4-L1-1/EEPNNLMitigation value "0 1"`.

Use `apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])` to force re-application onto TOMs that are already in place. The template-type value is serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; if no specific TOMs are provided (empty list), all system TOMs are considered. The default template-type is serdes-template. Application of serdes-templates depends on the global flag being set: `set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true` (enabled/disabled, default disabled). On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively, only from that moment onward, which is why apply-template is the way to push them onto already-installed pluggables. Example: `apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1`. Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: `commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]`. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version; the confirmation therefore acts as a 'persist' trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm with `commit persist` or abandon with `commit cancel`. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit the commands must carry the `-id=<id>` parameter, which identifies the commit confirmed, commit persist and confirmed cancel commands. All of these must be run in Candidate Configuration mode, entered with `configure`. `commit -m=<message>` attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use `show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]`, then pipe it through display commands: `show config | display commands`, and store the result for later use as a CLI script to restore the system configuration. `show config` displays only non-default configuration; anything left at its default value is skipped. The output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. To narrow it, supply an entity-id (the instance ID of the entity whose configuration you want) or, if all entities of a given type are relevant, an entity-type instead. The saved script can then be replayed, for example with `configure from-script=<script>`.

It depends on the target you pick. `configure <target>` takes exclusive or shared, and the default is exclusive: in exclusive mode only your session can make changes to the candidate configuration, whereas in shared mode multiple sessions can change the candidate configuration. The command runs from Operational mode and switches you into Candidate Configuration mode. You can also control the candidate's starting point: by default the Candidate Datastore starts from a copy of the Running Datastore; `from-default` starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration from the candidate; `from-script=<script>` imports configuration from a text file of CLI commands; `from-commit=<commit-id>` initializes from a past commit-record, which is only available when the Commit Repository feature is available, that is when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: `configure exclusive`.

Use `show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]`, which shows the current values of the advanced parameters that are actually running on the system, as opposed to `show advanced-parameter`, which shows what you configured plus its status. `show current-advanced-parameter` with no AID lists them all; `show current-advanced-parameter-1-7-L1-1/*` restricts the output to one optical carrier. The parameters are optical-carrier-name (string), current-advanced-parameter-name (string) and value (string, the value running on the system). The two views can differ: the guide's sample output flags a PMDEquUpdSpeed running value as not the configured value, and notes that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified since it is to be supported in a future release. Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

No, not everything. `clear [-f] database` performs a full wipe of database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system; it is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; for a secure wipe or factory default use the `clear system` command instead.
