Three clear-type values exist, default full: full resets the database to factory defaults; keep-networking wipes the database but keeps network configurations; initialize-from-script wipes it and initializes from a pre-stored .cli script (script parameter, absolute path or filename in /storage/scripts). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user (0..64 chars) and new-admin-password, and can only be triggered by the SA user. -f forces without confirmation. Transient alarms after the controller card reboot should be ignored.

Use `db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>` from Operational mode. The type parameter defines the protection mode to be configured and takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption; encryption-with-integrity is the one that adds the integrity protection on top of encryption. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The command automatically reboots the controller, for example `db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity` enables the integrity check for the system database and reboots the controller. You can verify the result with `show db-protection-scheme`, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is noted as changeable via the db-migrate RPC; integrity-algorithm will then read hmac-sha2-512 instead of none.

Use `show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]` and read integrity-status, which indicates the status of the integrity check and takes passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled. The companion attributes are mode, the current protection scheme of the DB (encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity), which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC; integrity-algorithm, either hmac-sha2-512 or none; and encryption-algorithm, xts-aes-256-plain64, AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size. On a node still in encryption-only mode the output shows integrity-algorithm none and integrity-status disabled. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Run `diff [-t|-c] candidate`, which must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore and the current system configuration as created, deleted or changed objects, showing only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate configuration and 'old' data is the current system configuration. Output forms: plain diff style, where + is an added object or new value and - is a deleted object or old value; side-by-side table with the -t flag; as CLI commands that reproduce the candidate changes with the -c flag; and the list of commands being executed with the -d flag. So `diff -c candidate` gives you the change as commands. `diff commit <id> [<id>]` compares a commit-record with the running configuration or another commit-record, and is available only when commit-records exist (commit-tracking enabled) or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run `discard-changes`. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags, and its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode, so it is only available once you have entered the candidate with `configure`. Note the scope: it throws away the entire candidate datastore, not a selected subset of edits. If instead you want to review what you staged before deciding, use `diff [-t|-c] candidate` from Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode first, and if you want to commit but keep an automatic escape hatch, use `commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>]`, which rolls back to the pre-commit version if not confirmed within the timeout (default 10 minutes).

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care. The commands are `add extended-config-<name>`, `delete extended-config-<name>` and `show extended-config-<name> [description]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Using it requires knowledge of the extended-config name on the user side, and the name must match a name known by the system; name is a string of length 0..64. Before adding one, read its description attribute (string, length 0..255), which is provided by the system and states the description of the extended-config and its effect in the system.

Check the service-impact attribute in the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with `show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]`. service-impact identifies whether applying that parameter change causes service impact and reads service-affecting or non-service-affecting; if it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock/maintenance operation or other relevant operations first. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change: no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. The same record gives supported-values (list of ranges or discrete numbers), type, direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive) and multiplicity (uint8, how many values you must enter). All attributes are read-only. Example: `show golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/EEPNNLMitigation`.

Run `lock` from Operational mode. It locks database access to the current session and grants exclusive write access to that CLI session; it is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, any other session (CLI or another type) that tries to make a configuration receives an error, and a lock is not possible if another session is already holding it. The lock is released either by the `unlock` command or by closing the session that performed the lock, whether explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or by inactivity time-out. Only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock; unlocking a non-locked database or one locked by another session fails. After unlock, any session can configure again and take a new lock. Both commands accept only the -h help flag.

A named-value-set is addressed as `named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that named-value-set. It holds a value item, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The commands are `add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]`, `set ... [value <value>]`, `show ... [value]` and `delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`. All four are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Only if recovery from chassis storage is configured for it. `set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value>` takes disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration on this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual clear recovery-mode is needed, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the hardware), or auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the Node Controller automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service. Monitor with `show recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage] [restore-status] [backup-status] [last-backup] [next-backup]`. restore-status values are init (default), image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore; backup-status is successful, failed, in-progress or unknown.

`rollback commit [<commit-id>]` works both on the Running Datastore (the default) and on the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if the candidate is empty; that is in fact a way to initialize the candidate. So with changes already staged you must clear them first, for example with `discard-changes`. If no commit-id is given, the most recent commit-record is used. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record and replays them in order, from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It relies on commit-records, so the commit-tracking system-policy must be enabled.

`show commit` is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither holds on your node, there are no Commit Repository records to visualize. Enable the repository with `set system-policies commit-tracking enabled` (values enabled/disabled, default disabled); note that disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. The syntax is `show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]`, where <id> selects a specific commit-record, -n selects an exact number of records to obtain, and -s picks a timestamp and shows all records created since it. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]` and `show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. commit-tracking (enabled/disabled, default disabled) enables the commit-repository feature: with it enabled, all configuration changes made via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records that can be visualized, compared and rolled back. Disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records, and the Commit Repository commands are only available while it is enabled. writable-running is also enabled/disabled with default disabled; disabling the writable-running policy makes configuration via the running datastore impossible and forces use of the candidate: the CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 become read-only.

The db-passphrase. The system only accepts `take-snapshot` if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of the security-policies (`set security-policies db-passphrase`) or locally as a parameter of the command (`take-snapshot db-passphrase=***`). The passphrase must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters in accordance with the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax: `take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]`, Operational mode. db-instance takes temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; type takes db-backup (default) or system-backup; description is a string 0..128. Re-taking an existing named snapshot overwrites the existing file.

Use the template commands. A template is a single template entry: an object/attribute pair plus the value to be used as the default for that attribute. Syntax: add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>]; set/show take the same AID with optional attributes, delete template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> removes it. object is the object name (e.g. odu), attribute the attribute name (e.g. admin-state), and value is mandatory (e.g. lock). sequence-id is a number 1..65535 defining processing order, lower ids first. condition is optional and restricts application (e.g. service-type=OTU4); label is an optional string. Example: add template-1/FansInMaintenance object card attribute admin-state value maintenance condition card-type=FAN. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. apply-template applies them.

No. The template-group is a configuration group containing a list of template entries, created with add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>]. The enabled parameter takes true or false, and its default is true only if there is no other template-group enabled, so a second group is not enabled by default while one is already active. name and label are strings. show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label] displays the group and delete template-group-<name> removes it. Example: add template-group-1 adds and enables the group. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show templates. This command shows the configuration that defines the data model for the system templates, that is the overall view of templates on the node. It takes no parameters: the full syntax is simply show templates. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the individual pieces, use show template-group-<name> for a template group and show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition] for a single template entry.

No. The unlock command releases a database previously locked with the lock command, but only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a non-locked database, or a database that was locked by another session, the unlock command will fail. The one way it clears without you is automatic: a lock is automatically released if the session that performed the lock is closed. Syntax: unlock [-h], where -h displays help for the command. Access mode: Operational Mode. After the unlock, any session is able to perform configurations and to perform a new lock.

Yes. Use validate candidate <candidate> command <string>. It validates the contents of the specified configuration, that is any CLI command(s) used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging, or replacing content. candidate is the candidate datastore that is the target for validation; command is the command string to validate. If the command is validated, the command replies with OK; otherwise the command will fail. Multiple CLI commands can be provided in one call if they are separated with a semicolon. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: validate 'set ne altitude 600'.

A maximum of 7 rounds of additional-key-exchange can be configured, and the additional-key-exchange-id is in the range 1..7. Configuring them is optional. You must choose a unique key-exchange algorithm for each round, and the rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Syntax: add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. Port level (CHILD-SA) key exchange is derived from IKE. Configuring it takes the IKE session down immediately to renegotiate. For PQC safety configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm (ml-kem-512/768/1024; ml-kem-1024 recommended).

Use show data-path-encryption. This command shows the datapath encryption attributes. It takes no parameters, so the complete syntax is show data-path-encryption. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related global policy is set with the ikev2 command: set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <match|ignore>.

Use the encryption-algorithm command, whose AID carries the algorithm and key length as keys: add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>, or without the SPD entry name for the IKE SA form: add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>. Only add, show and delete exist. Permitted algorithm values: null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16, chacha20-poly1305. Permitted key-length values: none, key-length-128, key-length-192, key-length-256, with default none. number is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. Example: add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192.

Use add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number> integrity-algorithm <value> dh-group <value> [prf <value>]. integrity-algorithm and dh-group are mandatory on add; prf is optional. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. prf values: hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. number is the proposal number, 1..max. protocol-id is read-only with value IKE. Example: add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The top-level ikev2 object carries one attribute: data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy indicating whether the NE must validate the certificate subject alternate name to match the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are match and ignore; no default is listed. Syntax: set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>] and show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]. Example: set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Read host-card-encryption-capability on the ikev2-local-instance: it indicates whether the card on which this IKEv2 local instance is running supports the ability to do encryption. Values yes, no, unknown, default unknown, show only. The local address is governed by local-address-assignment-method (auto or manual, default auto, show only) and local-address, a local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, default 0.0.0.0, settable. Syntax: set ikev2-local-instance-<name> [scope <value>] [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [local-address <value>]; show adds host-card-encryption-capability, host-card, started-time, AID, oper-state and local-address-assignment-method. scope values: data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method. admin-state lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock. Example: set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132.

On ikev2-peer, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer: range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. re-auth-frequency is the re-authentication frequency: range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200. The stated rule is that re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency values must not be multiples of each other, and they must have a difference of a few minutes to ensure a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Companion attributes: re-key-fail-policy (kill traffic, continue traffic; default continue-traffic) with re-key-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds, default 0, and re-auth-fail-policy with re-auth-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds, default 0, which set how long the system waits before killing the SAs tied to this IKE SA. Set them with set ikev2-peer-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name> re-key-frequency <value> re-auth-frequency <value>.

Use add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number> dh-group <value> [integrity-algorithm <value>]. dh-group is mandatory on add; integrity-algorithm is optional. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. number is the proposal number, 1..max; ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32. Two read-only leaves appear in show: protocol-id, the protocol ID used in the IKE SA and IPsec SA proposals, value ESP (default ESP), and esn, Extended Sequence Number support, value esn. Example: add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256.

Yes. The ipsec-sa-re-key command supports time, byte and packet based re-keying of the IPsec child SA with the far-end peer: add ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> [frequency <value>] [bytes <value>] [packets <value>], with matching set, show and delete. frequency is the time based re-keying frequency, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. bytes re-keys based on amount of bytes transmitted, range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. packets re-keys based on amount of packets transmitted, either disabled or a number in the range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. So volume based re-keying by bytes is already on by default at 1 GB, while packet based re-keying must be enabled explicitly. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The action attribute on ipsec-spd-entry indicates the IPsec treatment given to the IP datagrams; permitted values are protect, bypass and discard, with default protect. Yes, it tunnels by default: mode indicates whether the IPsec session operates in transport or tunnel mode, values tunnel and transport, default tunnel. Syntax: add ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> priority <value> [description <value>] [action <value>] [ipsec-protocol <value>] [mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [esn <value>] [anti-replay-window <value>] [dynamic-ts <value>]. priority is mandatory (uint8) and gives precedence between SPD entries. ipsec-protocol is ESP. esn true/false, default true. anti-replay-window applies when action = protect, range 32..1024, default 64. dynamic-ts disabled/enabled, default disabled. alarm-report-control default allowed. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect.

Create an ipsec-traffic-selector under the SPD entry, then attach the addresses and ports to it. Syntax: add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]. next-layer-protocol indicates the inner (upper layer) protocol taken from the IPv4 protocol or IPv6 next header field: any (value 0), opaque (value 255), or a number in the range 0-255; default any. The traffic-selector name is a string of length 1..64 matching pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). The actual addresses and ports are then added as child objects keyed off this selector: local-subnet and remote-subnet for the prefixes, local-ports and remote-ports for the port ranges. Example: add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17.

Because the port range is part of the AID, not a settable attribute. local-ports only supports add, show and delete: add local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, with the same AID for show and delete. There is no set form, so to change a range you delete the old one and add the new one. start takes all, opaque, or a port number; stop takes a port number and defaults to 0. If the stopping port is not set, the system assumes the value is 0, and 0 is only accepted if the starting port is set to all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all, and for an individual port with start=stop=53, add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53.

Use add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>, under the traffic selector that belongs to the SPD entry. The prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only) and is part of the AID, so only add, show and delete exist: show local-subnet-.../<prefix> and delete local-subnet-.../<prefix>. There is no set form, so to change a subnet you delete it and add the replacement. ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32; the traffic selector name is a string of length 1..64. Example: add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That is governed by link-security-control on the macsec-entity, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. The permitted values are must-secure and should-secure, and the default is must-secure, so by default the link must be secured. Set it with set macsec-entity-<name> link-security-control <value> or supply it on add macsec-entity-<name> [supporting-facility <value>] [enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [link-security-control <value>] [replay-protection <value>] [replay-protection-window <value>]. enabled is true/false, default true. replay-protection is enable/disable, with replay-protection-window giving the number of packets in the window, range 0..4294967295, default 0. show macsec-entity-<name> also reports oper-state and negotiated-cipher-suite.

Set the pre-shared key on the macsec-mka object: set macsec-mka-<name> [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [mka-policy <value>] [connectivity-association-key <value>] [connectivity-association-key-name <value>] [psk-lifetime <value>] [psk-expiration-warning <value>] [psk-lifetime-enable <value>]. connectivity-association-key is the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and connectivity-association-key-name its name, both strings of length 0..64. Whether the local end is key server is read with the is-key-server attribute, values true/false, default false, via show macsec-mka-<name> [AID] [alarm-report-control] [label] [mka-policy] [is-key-server] [connectivity-association-key] [connectivity-association-key-name] [psk-configured-timestamp] [psk-lifetime] [psk-expiration-warning] [psk-lifetime-enable]. PSK expiry warning range is 1..173 days, default 14 days. Example: set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa.

On the mka-policy object, the MKA policy referenced by the macsec entity related to an ethernet facility. Syntax: add mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>], with matching set, show and delete mka-policy-<name>. macsec-cipher-suite selects the cipher suites for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation. sak-rekey-interval is the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0|30..65535, default 30s, so that is how often the session key is refreshed. key-server-priority is the key server priority used by the MKA protocol to select the key-server. confidentiality-offset specifies a number of octets in an Ethernet frame that are sent in unencrypted plain-text. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the re-auth command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>, where ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), given as a string. Access mode: Operational mode only. Examples: re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202, and re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2. The scheduled equivalent is the re-auth-frequency attribute on ikev2-peer (3600..604800 seconds, default 43200).

The re-key command performs an on-demand re-key on any of three targets: a data path encryption secure entity, an IKEv2 peer, or an IPsec child security association (Security Policy Database entry). Syntax: re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>. ipsec-security-association points to the IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and secure-entity points to the secure entity object (Child SA); all are strings. Access mode: Operational mode. Examples: re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1 and re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX.

Add the remote port range with start set to all: add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, for example add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. start accepts all, opaque, or a port number. stop is a port-number with default 0; if the stopping port is not set the system assumes the value is 0, and 0 is only accepted if the starting port is set to all or opaque, which is why all needs no stop value. Only add, show and delete exist for remote-ports, so a range is replaced rather than edited. A single port is given as start and stop, e.g. add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49.

Use add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>, added under the traffic selector of the SPD entry. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only) and forms part of the AID, so the command set is add, show remote-subnet-.../<prefix> and delete remote-subnet-.../<prefix>; there is no set form, so a change means delete then add. ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32 and the traffic selector name a string of length 1..64. Example: add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the sc-rx command, which shows the Receiving Secure Channel attributes: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The 'state' attribute is what tells you whether the channel is in use; it is the state returned by the MKA stack and takes the values in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). The AID combines name, a string of length 0..64, with index, the Receiving Secure Channel Index, a uint8. sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a 16-character hex-string. sc-rx is show-only and is available in both Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is show-only; there is no add, set or delete form. The syntax is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. name is a string of length 0..64 and index is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index, a uint8. sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. state is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, either in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. The certificate it presents is set with active-certificate-id, a string of length 0..128 holding the list of assigned certificates: set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>. For example set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client, or a comma-separated list such as set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. The in-use attribute (a leafref to ../active-certificate-id) shows which one is actually active. To require a certificate from clients, set verify-client-cert, which enables TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled means no client certificate is requested (the default), required means the client certificate is required and validated and must be used for TLS Mutual Authentication. Changes to verify-client-cert take effect only for new TLS connections and have no impact on existing ones. Other show-only attributes are type (server or client) and status (enabled or disabled); show secure-applications lists them all.

That is controlled by re-key-fail-policy on the secure-entity, which indicates the NE's policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful. Values are kill-traffic and continue-traffic, and the default is continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, the traffic-kill-offset attribute gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds and it defaults to 0. Both are settable on add and set, for example: add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300. The related re-key-frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer ranges 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. Every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16; encryption-key-length is key-length-256; integrity-algorithm is none; and dh-group, the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer, is ecp-521. The proposal number likewise has the single value 1, default 1. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. So the layer 1 wavelength encryption suite is fixed and you can only display it, not change it.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the pair <ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>: ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA). The tie to the encrypted entity is the associated-secure-entity attribute, the list of all SPD entries associated with that far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). Syntax: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. Example on 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Use the cdp command to manage manually configured CRL Distribution Points; each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Syntax: add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], plus set, delete, show cdp-<name> and show cdps. url is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>', for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true, false, default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh or updates are performed although existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval either takes the special enum value use-next-update, meaning the next refresh time comes from the current CRL's next-update field, or a string in the form '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]' such as 2w, '5d 12h' or '1h 7m 30s'. show also returns next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen, an Operational mode command: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. Validity is set by days, the number of days the certificate is valid for, which defaults to 365. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128, org-name a string of 1..64, common-name the IP or host name identifying the server (1..64), and subject the full certificate subject name (1..1024). When generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install (true/false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application that has no active certificate. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, which defines a prioritized set of rules mapping an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly, or matches on a specific issuer in the certificate's trust chain. Syntax: add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>], with set, delete and show. map-type is extract or map. field applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute used to determine the identity: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and gives the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked. priority ranges 1 to 255. issuer takes the value any and adds a restriction filtering certificates from a specific issuer. enabled defaults to True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Use the certificate command in Operational mode. To remove one: clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>. type is trusted, local or peer; id is the certificate ID, a string of length 0..128, and it must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type (press <tab> to list the certificate-ids that can be cleared). -f forces the command without confirmation, otherwise you get an 'Are you sure? [y/n]' prompt. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY, clear certificate trusted id=root. type also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, use show certificates, which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates imported by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations.

Use the clear form of the crl command with a clear-target that selects a class of CRLs: clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>. The targets are single-crl (remove the CRL named in <crl-name>; this is the default and <crl-name> is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), purge-invalid-crls (purge all invalid CRLs), purge-cached-crls (purge all CRLs that were automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension), and purge-all-crls (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale entries, use purge-invalid-crls, for example: clear crl purge-invalid-crls. To remove one by name: clear crl single-crl myCA-1. Use <tab> to obtain the list of CRL names that can be cleared. Check status first with show crls or show crl-<name>, where status is valid, expired or future and type is cached or manually. The clear form runs in Operational mode; show also works in Candidate Configuration mode.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the 'pending-import' state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then given to an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded back into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that import happens the local-certificate stays in pending-import, which is also reported as the status attribute of local-certificate ('If CSR pending - pending-import'). Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] and so on. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256 (choices rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096, eccp128, eccp256, eccp384, eccp521); metadata-template defaults to generic; key-usage defaults to digitalSignature,keyAgreement and extended-key-usage to serverAuth,clientAuth. The subject must include the CN RDN. Operational mode only. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type accepts all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details and certificate-hierarchy, and defaults to all-certificate-hierarchy, so the trust chain view is what you get if you do not specify anything. Choose certificate-hierarchy for the chain of that one certificate, all-certificate-hierarchy for the full hierarchy, and certificate-details when you want only the certificate's own fields (version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, public key info and X509v3 extensions). certificate is a string naming the certificate to display, for example display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root; pressing tab after display-cert lists the available names such as local-certificate-server_cert and trusted-certificate-ca_root. The command also displays CSRs and runs in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport enables automated certificate management over HTTPS and replaces the manual CSR process; the device has an EST client that talks to a dedicated EST server. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]...] [[extended-key-usage=]...] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is the operation: cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca identifies the CA set for EST and defaults to 1. key-algorithm choices are eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic. Use http-user and http-password when no valid mTLS certificate exists. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via auto-re-enrollment on est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>]. auto-re-enrollment specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by that EST CA. It takes either a number of days before expiration from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the 'not after date' minus 'not before date' interval rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in increments of 10%, or disabled. The default is Disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until you set it. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example by expiring. The CA is pinned with explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port is set by server-port on the est-server command and defaults to 443. Yes, you can define more than one server: the key is <name>/<server-name>, so add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], with matching set, delete and show forms. priority defines the server's precedence, range 1 to 10; if omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence (the highest existing number) plus one, and if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. enabled is True or False and defaults to True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. server-address is the IP address of the EST server. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format directly into the NE: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]; import-certificate -h displays help. The certificate types are local-certificate, trusted-certificate and peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name by which the certificate will be known in the system. passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles and decodes encrypted input certificates. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle; for a single certificate it imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for instance /CN=Nokia yields trusted-certificate-Nokia-1 and trusted-certificate-Nokia-2. Examples: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>; import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=bundle-1 -i <string in PEM format>. Operational mode.

Show the key first and check its flags: show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates whether the key is in use in this FRU (true/false, default false), is-key-verified indicates whether the key is verified in this FRU (true/false, default false), and being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, meaning the system is in the process of deletion and will soon delete this ISK. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one: clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, where key-name is a string of length 0..64 and -f forces the command without confirmation. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1, then clear isk key-name=name. show works in both Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode; clear is Operational only.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys (KRKs) and KRK information: show KRKs lists them all, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] shows one, for example show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1. The attributes are CPU, the identifier for member CPUs on cards, starting at 0 (uint8); key-name, the name of the key, a string of length 0..64; key-serial-number; issuer-name, the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20; key-length, the key length in bits (uint16); and key-payload, the key payload in hex format, a string of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The KRK is the root key that signs ISKs, and each ISK reports its signer in its KRK-name attribute.

The key-replacement-package command shows key replacement package (KRP) attributes: show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. install-status indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system and takes the values not-installed, installing, installed and failed. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none; signature-payload is a hex string of length 0..1024; signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. KRK-name is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK, issuer-name is the CSA (Code Signing Appliance) name, a string of length 0..20, and KRP-version is the package version. The command is show-only and runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute on local-certificate: set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. revocation-mode controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, with auto as the default. Set force-revoked to make the node treat the certificate as revoked regardless of CRL or OCSP results, and force-unrevoked to force the opposite. The same attribute with the same values and the same auto default exists on peer-certificate. Check the result with show local-certificate-<id> revocation-mode status, where status reports pending-import, expired, revoked, untrusted, future or valid. Other settable attributes are alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and label (string 0..256). The id is a string of length 1..128. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use ocsp-server: add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>], delete ocsp-server-<name>, show ocsp-server and show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query]. Order is controlled by priority, a uint8 in the range 1..10 used to sort the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so priority 1 is tried first. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the port is optional, otherwise the default HTTP port 80 is used; the string is 0..1024 with pattern 'http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*)'. enabled (true, false, default false) controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status. last-query shows the timestamp of the last successful query, or never. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate that represents a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. The white-listed attribute is show-only, true or false with default false: if true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain (listed in the trust-chain attribute, a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id). Syntax: show peer-certificate[-id] [version] [serial-number] [subject-name] [issuer] [trust-chain] [valid-from] [valid-to] [status] ... [white-listed] [revocation-mode], and set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]. Settable attributes are only alarm-report-control (inhibited, allowed, default allowed), label (0..256) and revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked, default auto). status values include revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported.

SSH is off by default. On the ssh command, enabled enables direct access to shell via ssh and takes true or false with a default of false, so you must set ssh enabled true to turn it on. The port attribute is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell; its range is 1..65535 and the default is 8022, not 22. Syntax: set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>] and show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440 with no default; post-login-message is displayed after login, also 0..1440, and has a default warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key entry for that user. Each authorized key entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Syntax: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], with set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>], show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label] and delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user, a string of length 0..32; key-id is a unique identifier (name) for the entry, a string of length 1..64. public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format, '<key type><SPACE>...base64 encoded OpenSSH public key...<SPACE><comment>', a string of 0..2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is show-only: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTIt... Deleting prompts for confirmation.

The node's global SSHv2 host keys (used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 apps) are shown with 'show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint]'. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, more than one exists. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. public-key-algorithm values: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts in R9.0). public-key is PEM-encoded OpenSSH format, String 0..2048; label String 0..256; fingerprint-algorithm md5 or sha256; fingerprint String 0..95 as hex digit pairs. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Use 'show ssh-host-key' for the whole list, or e.g. 'show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521' for one.

ssh-keygen generates an SSH private/public key pair and the existing keys in the system are replaced with the newly generated pair. Syntax: 'ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>]', Operational mode only. -t is rsa, ecdsa or ed25519, default rsa. Key length via -b; if omitted the system uses the default for the key type. With secure mode disabled (security-policies/secure-mode): RSA supports 2048, 3072 or 4096 (default 2048); ECDSA supports 256, 384 or 521 (default 256). With secure mode enabled: RSA only 4096; ECDSA only 384 or 521 (default 384). ED25519 supports only 256 regardless of secure mode, and is available from R9.0. -l sets the key label; if not provided the label is the value of ne-id. Retrieve the resulting public key with 'show ssh-host-key'.

Add an SSHv2 known-hosts entry: 'add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]'. id is a unique name, String 0..64. address is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host; IPv4 is dotted-quad and IPv6 uses RFC 5952 canonical text, and either may carry a zone index after a % sign (numeric form is canonical; if absent the device default zone is used). public-key-algorithm: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 from R9.0). public-key is the OpenSSH/PEM-format host public key, String 0..2048. label is String 0..256. 'set ssh-known-host-<id>' can only change label; 'show ssh-known-host-<id>' and 'delete ssh-known-host-<id>' also exist. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The trusted-certificate object holds the X509v3 CA certificates (Root and Intermediate) trusted by the system. Syntax: 'set trusted-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]' and 'show trusted-certificate[-id]' with version, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length, public-key-type, signature-key-type, signature-hash-algorithm, certificate-bytes, key-usage, extended-key-usage, modification-time, revocation-mode, alarm-report-control, label. revocation-mode is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto. alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default allowed. label is String 0..256; id is string 0..4096; version is v3. Certificates are removed with the 'clear certificate' command, not with a delete on this object. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'terminate cable-id' (Operational Mode) to stop all running CableID verification tests. Because verification runs on a port-pair basis, the test can only be stopped after the current port-pair verification completes and before the next port-pair starts: the in-flight port-pair runs to completion, then the test exits. The maximum delay to terminate is therefore one port-pair verification time. The test is known to be terminated once cable-id-status cable-id-state changes to idle, so after issuing the command use 'show cable-id cable-id-status' to confirm the cable-id entity is back in the idle state. The show/terminate pair is documented under the cable-id command ('show cable-id', 'terminate cable-id'), which takes no parameters; show is also available in Candidate Configuration mode, terminate only in Operational Mode.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by the CAD10A and RD20TM cards; the signal is passed transparently in the OPSM. A CableID path starts at the end A port and terminates at the end Z port, where the signal is sourced/terminated, that is at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. Accordingly, 'show cable-id-path-<name>' reports card-type-a and card-type-z with values RD20TM or CAD10A, plus port-a and port-z as port AIDs. The card type is derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at the port-A/port-Z attribute: when a fiber-connection is created, the CableID function checks whether it lands on a port of a CableID capable sled and, if so, captures that card type into the CableID path topology. In R8.0.1 the supported sleds are CAD10A and RD20TM.

Yes. cable-id-status is the container holding the process status and progress of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you are allowed to issue 'show cable-id cable-id-status' at any time to query progress. Syntax: 'show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. cable-id-state values: idle (verification not running), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths), running-no-switching (running only for the active path); default idle. test-progress is a string 0..255, default 'None', showing 'Not applicable' if cable-id-state is disabled, or 'N out of M completed' while running, where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number already completed. Example output: cable-id-state idle, test-progress '1 out of 1 completed.'

Each carrier can discover up to one node. It is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. View the result with 'show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]'. local-carrier is the local carrier instance that discovered the neighbor, string 0..16. ne-id and ne-name are string 0..256, ne-type string 0..64, remote-carrier-id string 0..64 and is the AID of the remote carrier connected to the local carrier, implying a specific remote port id. last-update is date-time YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. The IPv4/IPv6 loopback addresses of the neighbor may be empty if not configured. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. degree-number is uint16 in range 1..20 and must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is uint32 in range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX, since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. port-name is an instance-identifier giving the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card; as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. Use 'show connection-ports*' to list all connection ports in the node, which returns rows such as connection-ports-1/1 with port-name port-1-3-dwdm-line1, or 'show connection-ports-5/1' for a single degree, which returns just the port-name (for example port-4-1-dwdm-line1).

Use the custom-tlv command, which shows the list of Organizational Specific TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameter information. Syntax: 'show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. lldp-port is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string 0..64. direction is ingress or egress. oui is the Organization Unique Identifier of the TLV, a hexadecimal representation of the 24 bit identifier, string 1..6. subtype is the sub-type identifier of the TLV within the scope of that OUI, string 1..507. The value attribute carries the TLV content.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS; although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Syntax: 'add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]'. Before R8.0 the user also had to set port external-connectivity to yes. From R8.0, with l0-mode-op set to slte, external fiber connections can represent intra-NE connections between RD20TM ADE ports or between CAD10A DWDM and RD20TM ADE ports; those entries must have scope set to cable-id (values general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose).

A fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, in an OADM/ILA topology. An external-fiber-connection represents a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, and it is set autonomously by TNMS (manual configuration is possible but not recommended). fiber-connection takes name (String 0..64), label (0..256), src-port and dst-port as instance identifiers, and fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way, default two-way. external-fiber-connection instead identifies endpoints by string: src-node-id and dst-node-id (0..256, logically the ne-name), src-card-name/dst-card-name (0..64), src-port-name/dst-port-name (0..128), and adds the scope attribute (general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose).

Yes. icdp is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol, and its global-switch flag, which enables icdp, has values true or false with a default of true. Syntax: 'set icdp global-switch <true|false>' and 'show icdp [global-switch]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: 'set icdp global-switch true' enables icdp. The related discovery results are viewed with the carrier-neighbor command, where each carrier can discover up to one node.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface, part of the Inter NE inter-op feature. It provides an API-based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example between a transponder such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40 and a line system such as FLEXILS, using gRPC server/client as the core mechanism. When the INCI service is enabled the gRPC server is started and bound to the local IP address; when an INCI neighbor instance is configured, gRPC client sessions are established. It is not running by default: 'set inci [inci-enabled <true|false>]' with inci-enabled defaulting to false. Enable it with 'set inci inci-enabled true' and check with 'show inci [inci-enabled]'. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Compare the provisioned name against the name the remote NE reports. On 'add inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> neighbor-address <value> configured-node-name <value> [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>]', configured-node-name is the user provisioned name of the remote NE and is used to compare against the discovered-node-name, which is the name of the remote NE as sent by the remote NE. Both are string 0..128. 'show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id>' also returns discovered-node-id, the node ID of the remote node as received from it (string 0..12), plus neighbor-address, neighbor-port, connection-status, alarm-report-control and oper-state (enabled or disabled). neighbor-id is the node-ID AID of the provisioned neighbor; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Both timers are attributes of interface-neighbor: 'set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. discovery-cycle-time is the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent, range 30..300 seconds, default 30. discovery-timeout is the time after which discovery is considered failed; when it occurs, neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout. Its range is 300..1800 seconds, default 300. discovery-enabled turns discovery on or off on the local interface, true or false, default true. neighbor-adjacency-state values are blackout, discovery, holding, unknown, default unknown; oper-state is enabled or disabled, default disabled. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. The links container within the topology is dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command is simply 'show links', with no parameters, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The related nct-connection command works the same way: it shows existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE and those links are also dynamically filled in by the system. Existing topology neighbor information can be removed manually with the 'clear topology' command.

The lldp object carries a single attribute, hold-on-timer, which is the time to keep neighbor information in case the neighbor does not send an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV. It is a number of seconds and defaults to 900. Syntax: 'set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]' and 'show lldp [hold-on-timer]', both in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: 'set lldp hold-on-timer 60'. On a per-neighbor basis, 'show lldp-neighbor' reports ttl, the number of seconds until the remote system information expires; if the remote system does not provide a ttl value, that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer.

'show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]' shows the LLDP local system information sent on an lldp-port. On the 1830 GX: chassis-id-subtype is chassis-component and chassis-id is the chassis serial number; port-id-subtype is local and port-id is the port AID; port-description is the port name; system-name is the NE name; and system-description is the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> _ build <software label>'. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities take the values router and bridge. All string attributes are 0..255. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: 'show lldp-local-info' or 'show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4'.

No, the egress direction is not supported. 'show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction>' takes direction as the direction in which the neighbor was detected, and the only value is ingress, for example 'show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress' or 'show -r lldp-neighbor-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4/ingress'. The same restriction applies to lldp-port-statistics, whose direction is also ingress only. The lldp-neighbor information is kept indefinitely, until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user. Available attributes include last-update, age, chassis-id-subtype/chassis-id, port-id-subtype/port-id, port-description, system-name, system-description, supported-capabilities, enabled-capabilities and ttl. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. All counter values in an lldp-port-statistics entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. The only thing that stops them is administrative state: all statistical counters associated with a particular port on the local LLDP agent become frozen whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. Syntax: 'show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-change-time] [last-clear-time] [total-ageouts] [total-discarded-frames] [error-frames] [total-frames-in] [total-frames-out] [total-discarded-tlvs] [total-unrecognized-tlvs]'; direction is ingress only, egress is not supported. total-ageout counts the times a neighbor's information was deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL expiry. Counters default to 0; last-clear-time defaults to 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

Use 'show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]', which shows NCT connectivity information, that is the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE. These links are dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. src-chassis-state and dst-chassis-state take the values node controller, provisioned and unprovisioned. src-port and dst-port must be NCT ports: for a commissioned chassis they are the port AID, and for an unprovisioned chassis they take the format '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>'. Similarly src-chassis and dst-chassis are the chassis AID if commissioned, or the chassis serial number if unprovisioned. All are string 0..64. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The sndp command has a single attribute, sndp-enabled, which is the switch controlling the sndp feature. Values are true or false, with a default of true, so the feature is on unless disabled. Syntax: 'set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]' and 'show sndp [sndp-enabled]', both available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'show sndp sndp-enabled'. The related per-interface control is interface-neighbor, whose discovery-cycle-time attribute sets the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent (30..300 seconds, default 30) and whose discovery-enabled switch turns discovery on or off on a given local interface.

'add submarine-link-<name> src-node-id <value> src-port-name <value> dst-node-id <value> dst-port-name <value> degree-target-tx-power <value> [...]'. The mandatory attributes are src-node-id and dst-node-id (the NE names of the endpoint nodes, String 0..256), src-port-name and dst-port-name (the OTS dwdm-line port of the degree, String 0..128), and degree-target-tx-power, the target launch power at the ROADM into the primary fiber. fiber-length is the fiber length in km of the associated fiber pair ID, decimal64 in range 0..25000 km, default 0, and does not include the length of branch segments. Optional attributes include label, src/dst-card-name (0..64), link-name, fiber-pair-id, segment-list (0..512), bu-segment-index (uint16, default 0), rx/tx-fiber-type, gsnr in dB, degree-expected-rx-power, commissioning-snr-margin, launch-condition (flat-tx or pfib, default pfib), allocated-spectrum-list (start/end frequency pairs, max 32 elements), and fiber-connection-type, which is two-way only for submarine links (default two-way).

supporting-fiber-connection shows the list of fiber connections supporting a given entity. Syntax: 'show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]', available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. name is the name of the entity, String 0..64, and fiber-connection-list is an instance-identifier giving the supported fiber connection path. It is used by CableID: 'show -r cable-id-path-<name>' displays the supporting-fiber-connection container and its fiber-connection-list along with all the cable-id-path parameters for the port-pair, for example 'supporting-fiber-connection-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6' with fiber-connection-list 'supporting-fiber-connection-R1'.

Use clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>. It manually removes existing topology neighbor information. The target may be an lldp-neighbor instance (discovered via LLDP), a carrier-neighbor instance (discovered via ICMP), or an lldp-port-statistics instance (details associated with an LLDP enabled port). target is an instance-identifier and is used only with clear; there is no default. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Tip: type 'clear topology <tab>' to list valid topology objects. Example: clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1. The companion show topology takes inci, links, lldp, icdp or sndp. Access mode is Operational Mode; Candidate Configuration Mode only for the show command.

Use verify [-f] [type-select=]<value> [[target-select=]<value>] [allow-switching]. type-select currently supports only fiber-connection. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if omitted, verification runs on all paths. If the port is in multiple CableID paths, all of them are checked. allow-switching is boolean, default false: false verifies active paths only (no system initiated switching), true lets CableID initiate switching on the OPSM so active and inactive paths are both verified, so use false when the system is in service. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. The command prompts for confirmation (-f skips it), raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE, and is non-blocking: check progress with show cable-id-status. Example: verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade3 allow-switching=true.

Use the bert command in Operational Mode: bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10, then bert stop test-id=TestX. test-id is alphanumeric and is system generated if you omit it, but it is mandatory for bert stop. test-signal-type: none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV, scrambled-idles; 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV. test-signal-monitoring-type adds fec-frames (CarrierCTP). Directions are ingress or egress. test-duration is in seconds, min 10 up to 1000 hrs; default 0 means indefinite. Also bert get and bert delete by test-id, resource or AID. Multiple simultaneous BERTs may run on a facility if each meets the pre-conditions.

The cid-ptp facility is created by the system when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A; managed-by is system and only user-created facilities can be user deleted, so you do not create it yourself. It supports the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. Only set and show are offered: set cid-ptp-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] and show cid-ptp-<name> with supporting-card, supporting-port, AID, oper-state, avail-state, managed-by, used. admin-state is not editable, the only supported value is unlock, and CableID operation is not affected by it. used is true when CableID functionality is supported (default false). label is a string 0..256. Example: show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid or show cid-ptp-1-6-spu. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The Digital Coherent 400ZR eth-zr facility is auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type shows 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) and rate is 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type is settable with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7; default is ofec. Degrade thresholds are in average BER over range 0.000000001..0.1: fdd-threshold default 0.0195, fdd-clear-threshold default 0.01062, fed-threshold default 0.0206, fed-clear-threshold default 0.01125. fdd-monitoring and fed-monitoring are enabled/disabled, default disabled. link-degrade-indication shows none, local-degraded, remote-degraded or local-and-remote-degraded. Example: set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000.

The ethernet facility attribute max-packet-length sets the maximum transfer unit in octets. On the 1830 GX G30 the range is 1280..18000 octets; on the 1830 GX G40 the range is 1518..18000 octets. The default is 1518. Set it with set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value> and read it with show ethernet-<name> max-packet-length. Two restrictions apply: max-packet-length is configurable on card level only and applies to all interfaces in that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet count in 100GbE PMs. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show facilities. It displays the system facilities, that is the list of facilities currently present on the node. It takes no parameters, and the only form is show facilities; access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. On a 1830 GX G40 node the output lists instances such as super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni and odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1. For per-facility detail, run the show command of the individual facility type, for example show ethernet-1-4-T2.

The fc facility (set fc-<name> / show fc-<name>) carries the Fibre Channel specific settings. fc-type is read-only and reports FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G or FC32G. tts enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support for the 32GFC client, values enabled/disabled, default disabled. laser-toggling-for-tts enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled or disabled for the 32GFC client, values enabled/disabled, default enabled. The rest are the common facility attributes: label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (GMP default, BMP, openZR+, FlexE-4x100G, GFP-F, GFP-F-extOPU2, AMP, iGMP, none), loopback (none/facility/terminal), loopback-mode, test-signal-type, test-signal-direction (default ingress) and test-signal-monitoring.

On the flexo facility, foic-type is a read-only attribute showing the FOICx.k interface: foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, default foic4.8. FOICx.k means k parallel lanes carrying a FlexO-x interface, where order x is the rate in units of 100G, per G.709.3 FlexO-LR and G.709.1 FlexO-SR. fec-type is also read-only with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec and noFEC, default ofec. resource-mode is settable and selects the resource mode: ADM for add-drop, XC for add-drop with regen; default is ADM.
