Example: set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state, alarm-report-control, iid and the fdd/fed raise and clear thresholds. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

add flexo-group-<name> requires four mandatory attributes: carriers, rate, modulation-format and group-id. carriers is the list of carriers bound to the facility, a string of length 1..32. rate is the carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s. modulation-format is one of not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM, BPSK. group-id indicates the interface group instance the FlexO-x interface belongs to and must be unique in the NE, range 1..1048575. Optional on add are label (0..256), admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and fec-type (not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7; default ofec). set additionally accepts expected-gid, flexo-type, loopback and loopback-mode. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

high-speed-monitoring has just two attributes, both set and show: enabled and port. enabled is the user configurable switch that turns high speed monitoring on or off, values true or false, default false. port is the user configurable port used by the function, a uint16 in the range 1..max with default 57500. Syntax is set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>] and show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

interlaken represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface facility; it is a system created facility (managed-by is system only). capacity is a read-only attribute giving the total capacity for the interlaken interface, 500 Gbit/s, which is also its default. The only editable attributes are label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited; default allowed) and loopback (none, facility for a test towards the facility side, terminal for a test towards the terminal side; default none). show also returns supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, AID, oper-state and avail-state. Example: set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

On line-ptp, auto-in-service-enabled is the auto-in-service switch for the facility, values true or false, default false, available on add, set and show. valid-signal-time is the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal and is used by the auto-in-service mechanism; the range is 1..7200 minutes and the default is 480. remaining-valid-signal-time is read-only and shows the actual time left before the facility is automatically enabled by the auto-in-service mechanism, also in the 1..7200 minute range. Set them with add or set line-ptp-<name> auto-in-service-enabled <value> valid-signal-time <value>. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. When auto-in-service is running, avail-state can report auto-in-service.

They are two different commands. network-xconnect is show only: show network-xconnect lists the services of the multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE; it has no parameters and runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. nw-xconnect is the configurable object: add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>], plus set (rate only), delete and show nw-xconnect-<name> [AID] [oper-state] [avail-state] [endpoint1] [endpoint2] [xcon-type] [rate]. So use nw-xconnect to create, modify or remove an individual user channel cross-connection, and network-xconnect to list the commissioned cross connections on the node.

nw-xconnect supports four xcon-type values and none of them joins a GCC to an OSC: L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0, L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC; the default is L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0. GCC to GCC uses add nw-xconnect-<name> xcon-type L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 endpoint1 comm-channel-ch1 endpoint2 comm-channel-ch2; OSC to OSC uses xcon-type L1-OSC-TO-OSC with two OSCX-5 comm-channel endpoints, for example endpoint1 comm-channel-2-5-dwdm-line1-OSCX5 endpoint2 comm-channel-2-5-dwdm-line2-OSCX5. endpoint1 and endpoint2 are mandatory instance-identifiers at creation. rate is the maximum user channel bandwidth, 1..20 Mbps, default 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC.

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created; when a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use show odu to determine whether the ODU exists. What you create yourself are the low order ODUs, ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G), which the XCONs are mapped into, and the documented pre-condition is that the super-channel must be added before low order ODUs can be added. The class attribute is system-set: high-order for the top-most ODUCn/ODUk the system creates, low-order (the default) for children, mapped for a mapped client signal. Create a LO-ODU with add odu-<name> odu-type <value> parent-odu <name> [time-slots <value>] [trib-port-number <value>], for example add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80.

Yes. odu-diagnostics is keyed as odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> where direction is ingress or egress, and each direction has its own values. Use add or set odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> with tx-tti, expected-tti, tx-sapi, tx-dapi, tx-operator, expected-sapi, expected-dapi and expected-operator. tti-style selects the format: ITU-T-G709 (default), where the TTI splits into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes, or proprietary, a single 64 byte string. tx-tti and expected-tti take a hex string with 0x prefix (1..130 characters) or printable ASCII (1..64); SAPI and DAPI are 1..15 ASCII (hex 1..32) and operator 1..32 ASCII (hex 1..66); the expected-* fields default to empty. Example: set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPIDAPI-OPER.

Yes, FEC is on by default. On the otu facility fec-mode is the configured Forward Error Correction mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client with values enabled or disabled, and the default is enabled. fec-generation-mode, the FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver, is also enabled/disabled with default enabled. fec-type selects the FEC and takes not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 or ufec7; the default is ofec. All three are available on add, set and show, for example set otu-<name> fec-mode disabled or show otu-<name> fec-mode fec-generation-mode fec-type. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting attribute on otu-diagnostics to SAPI so the TIM alarm is raised only on a Source Access Point Identifier mismatch: set otu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI, for example set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI. The attribute indicates whether the TTI-Mismatch (TIM) alarm is reported or masked and, if reported, the criteria used. Values are disabled (default, alarm masked), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI_DAPI, SAPI_OPER, DAPI_OPER and SAPI_DAPI_OPER. Configure the expected value with expected-sapi and keep tti-style at ITU-T-G709 (the default) so the TTI is split into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes. Each direction (ingress, egress) has its own values.

The stm facility reports stm-type, the type of SDH signal (STM-N), and the supported values are STM-16 and STM-64; it is a read-only show attribute. The name of the facility is the Synchronous Transport Module N, for example N=16 or 64, per ITU-T G.691. Related trib-ptp service-type values also list STM16 and STM64. Settable STM attributes are label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tx-tti and expected-tti (tti-64), loopback and loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), test-signal-type, test-signal-direction and test-signal-monitoring. Example: set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP.

The trib-ptp attribute tributary-disable-action defines what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). tributary-disable-holdoff-timer sets the hold off time of the client shutdown or replacement signal in the egress direction, range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff. Related switches: near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true). Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

Create a Layer 1 digital cross connect with add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>]; source and destination are instance IDs of the two end-points, for example add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1. direction only supports two-way, which is also the default. payload-type covers 100GBE, 400GBE, OTU4, 100G, ODU2, ODU2e and empty. set only changes label and circuit-id-suffix; delete xcon-<name> removes it, and only user created XCONs can be user deleted. protection-type is a read-only show attribute representing the protection this XCON has, with values y-cable, snc-n, snc-i and unprotected; the default is unprotected. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

An L2-bridge is identified by bridge-name, a string of length 0..64 used in the entity name L2-bridge-<bridge-name>. Only set and show are available: set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>] and show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]. There are just two configurable attributes: chassis-name, a leafref giving the chassis associated with this L2 bridge, and description, a string of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. Neither has a default. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the clear app command: clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>. app-name is the third party app name. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, otherwise the command prompts. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. clear app is the only form documented for the app entity; to control rather than remove a third-party application, use the appctl command with commands restart, netls or exec.

Use appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]. app-name is the third party app name, a leafref to the third-party-app app-name under system sw-management. command is mandatory and takes restart (restarts the third party application), netls (shows the list of subnet networks used by the containers) or exec (executes a third party application operation given in parameters). target says whether the command is executed for the entire system or for a chassis/card AID; it is a string or the value system, and the default is system. parameters are optional values passed with the command, applicable when command is restart or exec, with max-elements 50. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Use the `call-home` command in Operational Mode: `call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>`. It executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server, forcing an immediate connection attempt. If the dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state, the command forces an immediate attempt and will not wait for the retry interval before trying again. The pre-condition is that the dial-out server must already be configured for the command to execute properly. The dial-out-server-name parameter is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). Examples: `call-home collector-x`, `call-home dialoutservername`, and `call-home -h` for help. Note `auto-connect false` on a dial-out-server still allows manual connection via the call-home RPC.

Use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` (Operational or Candidate Configuration mode) to list configured telemetry subscriptions with encoding and transfer-mode. The `encoding` attribute specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device, and may be specified for all data or per-RPC if the target supports it; permitted values are json, bytes, proto, ascii and json-ietf, default json-ietf. The `transfer-mode` attribute specifies the data transfer mode to the target device: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off by the target), or poll (values sent in response to a poll request), default stream. Related attributes include session-protocol (gnmi, default gnmi), session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc) and updates-only (true/false, default false).

No, YANG data models are not all loaded by default. The `data-model` object has an `enabled` attribute whose default is false; setting it true loads the model so it can be used via the management interfaces, and setting it false unloads it. Turn one on with `set data-model-<name> enabled true`, where name is the model name (String, length 0..256). Inspect models with `show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]`, or just `show data-model` to view all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. `description` (String, length 0..256) is a show-only attribute. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A dial-out-server's `retry-policy` is the retry policy applied after a timeout, with values progressive-back-off, retry-then-stop and retry-forever; the default is progressive-back-off. `retry` is the number of retries and is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop: Integer range 0..5, default 3. `timeout` is the time before the next retry, Integer range 1..255 seconds, default 10, and is not applicable for progressive-back-off (which has a dynamic timeout). The session `port` defaults to 4334, the default for the netconf protocol over ssh, and is configurable in the range 1..65535. `protocol` is netconf or restconf (default netconf) and transport is ssh. Example: `set dial-out-server-callhome1 auto-connect false retry-policy retry-then-stop port 4889 timeout 200 retry 5`.

Yes, gRPC/gNMI is enabled by default. The `grpc` object's `enabled` attribute enables or disables the gRPC management protocol and defaults to true. The `port` attribute is the port which listens for gNMI access via gRPC where gRPC is enabled, and defaults to 50051. Also configurable is `gnmi-get-encoding-granularity`, which controls the granularity of data in gNMI Get responses when encoded with JSON: per-path puts all path data in one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. Use `show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]` and `set grpc enabled false` / `set grpc enabled true`. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

NETCONF listens on `port` for access via ssh, a port-number (uint16, range 1..65535) with default 830. The `hello-timeout` attribute specifies the number of seconds that a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; the session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that many seconds elapse. It is a uint16 in the range 1..3600 seconds with a default of 2. Configure with `set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [hello-timeout <value>] [annotate-cli-name <value>] [static-info-in-notifs <value>]` and view with `show netconf`. NETCONF `enabled` defaults to true, and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session.

RESTCONF itself is enabled by default (`enabled` true), but plain HTTP is not: `http-enabled` defaults to false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. `https-enabled` defaults to true. Ports are `http-port` default 8080 and `https-port` default 8181, both in range 1..65535. Session lifetime is controlled by `cookie-timeout`, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, in the range 1..300 minutes with a default of 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: `set restconf cookie-timeout 10`. `show restconf` also displays the read-only `api-root` (root of the RESTCONF API, String length 0..64).

Use `show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]`. The `snmp-engine-id` is a show-only attribute giving the SNMP EngineID of the NE; it follows EngineID format 3 as defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the NE's MAC address pool (String, length 0..256). `engine-boot-count` is also show-only and counts how many times the engine has restarted (Number, uint16, default 0). The settable attributes are `enabled` (true/false, default true, global SNMP access) and `port`, the port on which the NE listens for SNMP requests (range 1..65535, default 161). Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object, not here.

No. The `community-string-access` attribute of snmp-community defines the SNMP access right of the community string, and read-only is the only permitted value as well as the default. Create a community with `add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]`, where `name` is the community name, distinct from the community string itself (String, length 0..64), `community-string` is the string itself (String, length 1..32, mandatory), and `enabled` turns the community-string on or off (true/false, default true). Example: `add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true`. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The trap-community-string lives in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`. `target-name` is String 0..32. `snmp-version` may be v2c or v3, default v2c. `trap-community-string` is the community string used for SNMP traps, String 0..32, default infinera. `target-port` is the UDP port number, range 0..65535, default 162, and `target-transport` is udp (only value, default udp). `snmpv3-user` applies only when snmp-version is v3. `enabled` defaults to true. `target-address` is the IPv4/IPv6 address or hostname of the target, optionally with a %zone index.

A new SNMPv3 user gets `user-sec-level` no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol `priv-protocol` may be DES, AES128, AES192 or AES256, with AES128 as the default. Authentication protocol `auth-protocol` supports only SHA (default SHA). Create with `add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]`; the user name is String length 1..32 and both passphrases are String length 8..64. Example: `add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123`.

The `subscription-path-mode` attribute of subscription-path controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined, on-change, or sample; the default is target-defined. View with `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]`. `sample-interval` is the time in milliseconds between samples of a telemetry data source (default 0, meaning optional); for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset, the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. `heartbeat-interval` (milliseconds, default 0) is the maximum interval between updates; for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset and heartbeat-interval below 10 seconds, the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. `suppress-redundant` (true/false, default true) suppresses redundant updates.

Use `show subscriptions`. That is the entire syntax; the command takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It shows a list of subscriptions on the node. For the detail of telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>`, which exposes related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the per-path detail of a subscription, use `show subscription-path` or `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`, which exposes subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode, sample-interval, heartbeat-interval and suppress-redundant.

Telemetry is configured through the `telemetry` object, which is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry. The syntax is `show telemetry` and `set telemetry id <string>`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The object has a single parameter, `id`, described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, of type string with length 0..4096 and no default. The telemetry object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: `show telemetry` displays the telemetry subscription. Beyond that single `id` attribute, no further distinction between persistent and dynamic telemetry is stated; the associated subscriptions are viewed with `show subscriptions`, `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` and `show subscription-path`.

Use `show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]`, or `show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]`. The `state` attribute reports the third party app state with values running, stopped or failed, and its default is stopped. The `enable` attribute is the third-party-app enabled state: if enabled the app is started, and it is also enabled upon system restart; if disabled the app is stopped. Its values are true and false, and the default is false, so an app is not enabled by default. Other attributes are version (string 0..64), vendor (string 0..64), product (string 0..256) and information (string 0..1024). Set them with `set third-party-app-<app-name> ...` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `add <tab>` to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time. The `add` command creates a new managed entity in the system database; the entity id format varies by managed entity type. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided at creation, and if a mandatory attribute is not provided in the command itself the CLI automatically asks for it. Non-mandatory attributes can also be initialized by supplying attribute-value pairs. Syntax: `add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]`, with -v validating the command only (nothing created, replies 'OK' if valid), -m merging (best effort add: create if absent, update if present), -f forcing without confirmation, and -h for help. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with `add`. The guide lists the creatable entities (aaa-server, acl, card, dial-out-server, interface, snmp-target, tom, user, xcon and many more), each cross-referenced to its own command page.

Yes, by default. The `clear` command clears entries for the specified entity, and in all cases requires a user confirmation; a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, and -h displays help. Syntax is `clear [-f] <subcommand> ...` and the command runs in Operational Mode. The subcommands are alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, system, topology, dns, statistics. Note that `clear system factory-reset` with the `shutdown` option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes, via the `show-alarm-columns` attribute of the `cli` object, which defines the columns to display in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, `default-columns` to show the pre-defined columns, or `default-columns,<additional-details>` to show that additional column alongside the pre-defined ones. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect and takes effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: `set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3` and `set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action`. Other cli attributes are enabled (true/false, default true; CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port for CLI access via ssh (range 1..65535, default 22), read-only script-dir (String 1..80), and default-interactive-mode (true/false, default true).

Use `set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>`. The `cli-lines` attribute is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes display. Its range is 10..1000 with a default of 40. Width is set with `cli-columns`, the configurable number of columns used for display, range 80..4000, default 80. View with `show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]`. Examples: `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30` and `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-columns 100`. Also per-session are interactive-mode (true/false, default true, not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false).

Yes. The `connect` command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI. Syntax: `connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]`, available in Operational Mode. `target-address` may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or hostname if DNS is configured; it requires connectivity and is a mandatory attribute. `user-name` is a string of 0..64 characters. `port` is optional; by default port 22 is used, but another may be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Example: `connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022`, which then adds the host to the known hosts list and prompts for the remote user's password.

Yes, use the `convert` command: `convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. target-representation values are netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted (encrypts a string using security-policies/csp-passphrase), snmp-oids (OIDs for objects in a 'show' command) and netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing the SNMP request). The command should be enclosed in quotes; multiple CLI commands separated by ';' are merged into one payload where possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto-filled, only the password must be entered. Example: `convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'`.

No. The `default` command assigns default values to the targeted entities, which is useful to reset an entity after changes, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes that are only settable at creation. Syntax: `default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. If attributes are specified, only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation and -h shows help. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: `default user-peter`, `default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*`, `default alarm-severity-entry-*`, and `default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode`. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: `delete -b <object>` is the best effort delete introduced in R9.0. It only bypasses the check for object existence without returning a failure, so it does not fail if the object does not exist, whereas standard `delete <object>` does fail in that case. It has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Caveat: -b does not raise an error if the object is missing, but it may still produce other errors such as precondition failures. Syntax is `delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]`. In a script you will normally combine it with -f, which forces the command without confirmation, since delete otherwise displays a confirmation prompt. -v validates only, executing no deletion and replying 'OK' if valid. Deleting an entity also removes all its sub-level objects, and is rejected if the entity or its sub-level containers carry services or other traffic affecting configuration.

The `exit` command logs you out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided. Syntax: `exit [-h|-f]`, where -f forces the command without confirmation and -h displays help; access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as `exit -f`, that is, it exits immediately without the confirmation prompt. Example: `exit -f`.

Use the `expect` command, which ensures an attribute matches an expected value: `expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions, and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes. Wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. If the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: `expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123` and `expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*`.

Yes, use the export command: 'export [<variable>=[<value>]]'. Variables are referenced as ${variable} in any CLI command, which is especially useful in CLI scripts. The variable name can be any alphanumeric name; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. They do NOT survive logout: variables are locally defined per session and are removed after the session is closed. 'export SLOT_NUMBER=2' declares one, 'export SLOT_NUMBER=' deletes it, and bare 'export' lists all existing variables (output looks like export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154" / export MYUSERNAME="admin"). Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Both launch a Linux bash shell from the CLI and are Operational Mode only, and both accept a single command to execute instead of an interactive session; exit returns you to the CLI prompt. 'shell [-h] [shell command]' runs on the node itself, launched as the currently logged in user with that user's command access; access can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups, and certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted list includes /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a set of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). 'gshell [-h] [<cmd>]' instead launches the bash shell inside a Guest Container, and has a pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Example: gshell ls -l.

No. 'kill-session <session-id>' closes any established session independently of its type (CLI, NETCONF, etc), but the <session-id> must match an existing session and cannot match the id of your current session; to end your own session use the normal 'exit' command instead. The session-id is a string in the form '<ip-address>:<port>'. Use 'show session' first to display the list of current sessions and pick the id. Access mode: Operational mode. Example: kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212.

Use the message command: 'message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]'. By default the message is broadcast to all CLI sessions (target default = all), so 'message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"' reaches everyone. message content is a string of 1-4096 characters. The target values are: all (all CLI sessions), local (only local sessions: serial console or CRAFT), remote (only remote sessions, e.g. SSH), session-id (only one specific session), and username (all CLI sessions of a specific user). Example targeted form: message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36. Access mode: Operational mode. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only sent to CLI sessions.

Properties are type-specific, auto instantiated by the system but user configurable, addressed as property-<card-name>/<property-name>. Syntax: 'set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]' and 'show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]'. Two property-names are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures (values disabled, enabled; default disabled); and max-packet-length, the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO (range 1518 to 18000; default 1518). Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled.

Use run. Syntax: 'run task [[task-name=]<value>]' and 'run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]'. Pre-condition: the task or the script to be called must already be defined. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name; script-name is a relative path to the script directory, with optional arguments as a string. Flags: -q runs the script in quiet mode (only command output shown, otherwise both the command and its output are shown), -r executes the script as a declarative config script, replacing system configuration with the script content, and -e sets the error option: continue (default), stop or rollback. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: run task collect-diag; run script config.cli -e=stop -q.

Both add/set/show/delete user-configurable scheduled commands in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, and both share enabled (true/false, default true), command (string), command-type (CLI command), frequency, start-time, end-time and persistent (true/false, default true, meaning the task survives a system restart). 'task-<name>' is the fuller object: name is a string 0..64 characters, command is 1..1024 characters, and it adds label, alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and number-of-runs (no-limit or 1..65535, default no-limit, applicable when frequency is configured); its read-only show attributes are task-status (scheduled, disabled, finished, ongoing; default scheduled), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success or fail) and previous-output. 'scheduled-task-<name>' uses the same fields but exposes them via add/set with coarser values (task-status true/false default false, previous-result 1 or 2) and is listed with 'show scheduled-tasks'.

Only if you are an SA user. 'show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]' shows the currently established management layer sessions, but only SA users can access the list of all sessions; remaining users can only see their own session. session-id is the IP address and transport port of the session, or 'NA' if the session is initiated from the serial port. session-type values: cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui, gnmi. session-protocol values: telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https, http. RESTCONF sessions are visible in CLI when Cookie Based Authentication is used; that session has a keep-alive of 5 minutes by default, changeable with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. 'set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]' takes at least one attribute-value pair, all belonging to the same managed entity; if no entity id is given the currently scoped entity is used. Wildcards (*) set an attribute on multiple instances at once: as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*) and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). You can also use [] for ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]), and filters of the form <attribute>=<value>, e.g. 'set port port-type=line admin-state lock'. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates. Example: set port-1-4* admin-state lock.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups. 'shell [-h] [shell command]' is Operational Mode only and launches the Linux bash shell as the currently logged in user, allowing only the commands accessible to that user; exit the shell the usual way (for example the 'exit' command) to return to the CLI prompt. A single shell command can also be run inline, e.g. shell ifconfig, shell vi, shell editor. Certain commands/scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo'; the permitted set includes /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a list of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts (download.sh, install_os.sh, config_ip.sh, docker.sh, CopyLogsToUSB.sh and others). Use single quotes for composed commands: shell 'sudo netstat -alnp | grep sshd'.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request instead: give a specific <entity-id> or <entity-type>, add filters of the form <attribute>=<value>, or use wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*, admin* for admin-state) and ranges/lists (card-1-[1..4], interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Limit recursion with -r=<n>, which operates the command recursively for n levels down (full recursion if n is not provided). Other useful flags are -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only), -o (state/read-only only), -t (tabular), -l (long) and -d (show default values). Piping through '| more' displays long output page by page.

Yes for alarms and card insertion. 'simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])'. Trigger values: raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru, plug-out-fru, but note that plug-out-fru is not supported. Equipment simulation needs the holder-AID (string 1..64) matching the card slot or the tom port, plus the card type; subtype is optional. Alarm simulation needs alarmed-entity and alarm-type; if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location both default to auto (selected automatically by the system). The command works in a simulator and on a real system, but on a real system simulation cannot be done if it interferes with real HW, for example you cannot simulate plugout of hardware that is physically present. Access mode: Operational mode. Example: simulate plug-in-fru 1-5.

Yes. 'sleep <time in seconds>' specifies a delay, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number, so fractions of a second are allowed. 'sleep 1' waits one second and 'sleep 0.1' waits 100 milliseconds. The only flag is -h, which displays help for the command. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, so it can be used inside CLI scripts run with 'run script'.

Add a task with no frequency: a task with no frequency interval configured is a single-occurrence task (in scheduled-task the guide states that an empty frequency, the default, represents a single-occurrence task). Syntax: 'add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]'. start-time is the timestamp to start the task. The guide's own example is: add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once". Note: this requires that the file server xfr1 be configured before the command is used. Defaults: enabled true, persistent true (survives a system restart), command-type cli, alarm-report-control allowed, end-time never. Check progress with 'show task-<name>' fields task-status (scheduled/disabled/finished/ongoing), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success/fail) and previous-output.

'terminate' stops a running operation, Operational Mode. Forms: 'terminate location-led <entity>' stops a location led test previously started with activate on a chassis or a card (no effect if no test is active); 'terminate otdr [entity=]<value>' stops an ongoing OTDR measurement for the given port; 'terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>' stops a manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity, aborting the scan abruptly, restoring otdr ne function attributes and reverting ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state (if that state was fail, the PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED alarm is raised again); 'terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*' terminates WSS loopback on NMC entities, and all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated; 'terminate cable-id' stops CableID verification. Confirmation for CableID: the test is known to be terminated once cable-id-status cable-id-state changes to idle, checked with 'show cable-id cable-id-status'. Termination is per port-pair, so the maximum delay is one port-pair verification time.

'update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]' triggers a specific predefined update action on an object attribute rather than assigning an arbitrary value the way set does, and it is Operational mode only (set works in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). The type values are: span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates/re-evaluates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to under commissioning state; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to Ready for Service state. The last two apply to NE entities in SLTE systems. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line; update filter-insertion-date-now chassis.

Use the auxiliary commands tic and toc. tic starts a timer for the typed command, and toc displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Wrap a single command as 'tic;show log;toc'. For a list of commands (a script) put them on separate lines between the two, for example: tic / ;show log / ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 / ;toc. These are add-on auxiliary commands intended for evaluating the system response to a command or script.

Yes. Use 'help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]'. It searches the provided keyword(s) in all commands help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Partial keywords can be provided using a wild card, for example 'help -s inventory' or 'help -s data*'. The rest of the help system: '?' on its own displays the list of all available commands; 'help <command/container/attribute>' (e.g. help show) explains how the command, container or attribute can be used; '<command> ?' (show ?) lists the possible addressable parameters; '<command> -?' (show -?) lists the possible options; '<command> -h' (show -h) shows the complete help; '<command> <container> ?' shows the container's hierarchy sub-containers and attribute list; '<command> <attribute> ?' lists the attributes of the given container.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so an alias survives your logout and other operators see it. 'alias [<name>=<value>]' defines a more user-friendly alphanumeric string for one or more commands, a container, an attribute or values; 'alias' with no arguments prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Quotes must be used for multi-word values, e.g. alias sa='show alarm'; a single word alias is alias s=show. Aliases can reference other aliases, and the <name> of an alias can be used without resolving it by putting it in quotes. Remove them with the unalias command. Access mode: Operational mode.

'unalias -a' removes all defined aliases. Syntax: 'unalias -h', 'unalias -a', 'unalias [<name> ...]', so you can also remove specific ones (unalias foo, or unalias bar baz qux). Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users, because aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so clearing them affects every operator on the node, not just you. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Aliases can be added and visualized again with the 'alias' command. Access mode: Operational Mode.

'tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...])' controls this. Use -d=depth to set the maximum display depth, i.e. the number of levels to be displayed; if not specified, all levels are displayed by default, e.g. 'tree -d=2'. Use -a to display entity ancestors only, showing just the target entity along with all its ancestors, e.g. 'tree -a interface-DCN' or 'tree -a port usb'. -o displays a tree based on a YANG top node. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id, e.g. 'tree card-1-1'. Only managed entities are shown, including all existing instances, with no attribute names or values, and output uses the UTF-8 character set. You can also page it with 'tree | more'. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

All three change the currently selected managed entity and the effect is visible on the CLI path banner; all are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. 'edit [-h] <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]' navigates to any entity in the hierarchy; the entity IDs can be absolute (starting from the root of the system) or relative to the current entity shown in the path banner, and the attempt to edit a nonexistent entity instance will fail. Examples: edit port-1-5-T1, edit card-1-1, or relative edit chassis-1 slot-2. 'up [-h]' brings the current path up by one path level, to the parent, and supports no parameters; at the hierarchy top level it has no impact. 'top [-h]' brings the current path straight to the top of the managed entity hierarchy, [ne].

Use the history command. 'history [-h]' displays the current session's command history as a numbered list. Each command can be repeated using '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and '!!' repeats the previous command. To find a particular entry, filter the listing with piped commands, for example: history | include 'show'. Access mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The list covers the current session only.

Nothing happens: at the hierarchy top level the 'up' command has no impact. 'up [-h]' brings the current path up by one path level in the managed entity hierarchy, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent level, and the effect is visible on the CLI banner; the command does not support any parameters. So from [card-1-5], up goes to [equipment], and up again goes to [ne]; issuing up again at [ne] leaves you at [ne]. Related commands: 'edit' navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, 'top' navigates to the top of the hierarchy root. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

They do the same job, and the guide states each is the same as the other: both are piped commands (<command> | grep <filter> / <command> | include <filter>) that only display lines matching <filter>, do a case insensitive comparison (show | grep abc is equivalent to show | grep ABC), accept multiple words separated by spaces when enclosed in quotes, support regex, and can be chained with other piped commands. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> (number of lines of context to show after the actual match), -b=<n> (number of lines of context to show before the actual match) and -n (displays line numbers in the result). include takes only <filter> and -h. Related filters: exclude removes matching lines, begin starts output at a matching line, until ends output at a matching line.

Yes. Pipe a show into the `display` piped command with the `commands` mode: `<command> | display commands` renders the configuration as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, which is useful for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. The recommended form is `show config | display commands`, storing the result for later usage, which is the documented way to build a CLI script that can restore the system configuration. `show config` displays only non-default configuration (attributes at their default values are skipped) and is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the hierarchy gives the complete system configuration; syntax is `show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]` if you want to limit the scope. `show -r | display commands` also works. Other display modes are list (default), table, csv, keys-table, single-table, only-values, xml, json, xpath and interactive.

Yes. Chain the `begin` and `until` piped commands, which are explicitly documented as usable together to retrieve a sub-set of an output. `begin` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word: `<command> | begin <words>`. `until` displays the output ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word: `<command> | until <words>`. In both, <words> is the line to begin with / end with and may contain spaces if enclosed in quotes; `-h` displays help for the command. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command line, so pipe show into begin and then into until to get the span between the two lines.

Yes, use the `more` piped command, and yes, position matters: multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. Syntax is `<command> | more [-h]`, where <command> is any display command such as tree or show, and -h displays help. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, that is, the terminal size, except for the serial port case where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display pauses; press any key to resume or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space> and <tab>) shows the next page. Example of a filtered listing paged: `tree | include led | more`; also `show -r | more`.

It does not fail: with the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used, it is ignored. Syntax is `<show command> | sort [-h]` or `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`. `sort` with no parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. A list of attributes can be provided as parameters and is used for sorting; <attribute> is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output. To flip the order, use `-i`, which inverts the order and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. Examples: `show card | sort`, `show port | sort port-type`, `show odu | sort -i` (inverted order), and `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date` (sorted by user-group then last-login-date, inverted). `-h` displays help for the command.

Capitalisation does not matter and patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command filters out lines containing the given word or string: `<command> | exclude <filter>`. The <filter> does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed in quotes, for example `show | exclude 'ne oper'`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. `-h` displays help. Examples: `show | exclude ne`, `show led | exclude status`. The complementary commands are `include` and `grep`, which display only the matching lines (grep and include are the same command, and grep additionally supports -a=<n> lines of context after the match, -b=<n> before, and -n for line numbers).

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of a given command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`. More than one word can be provided. Without quotes the words are searched for separately, so `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` highlights 'odu4' and 'oduflex' independently. To mark up a whole phrase, enclose it in quotes so it is searched for as a sentence: <word> may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. You can mix both forms, for example `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` highlights the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the single word 'odu4'. `<command>` is any normal command that generates output, and `-h` displays help for the command.

Yes. The `linenum` piped command adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax is `<command> | linenum`, or `<command> | linenum -h` where -h displays help for the command. <command> is any display command such as tree or show. It takes no other parameters. Example: `show | linenum` displays the output with enumerated lines. As an alternative when you are already filtering, the `grep` piped command supports the `-n` option, which displays line numbers in the result (grep also takes -a=<n> for lines of context after the match and -b=<n> for lines of context before it).
